#9913. Playing with the STM32MP2

First off, an apology - this post is long overdue. I started writing it back even before the TCXO post, I think some time in December 2025. But then I ended up accidentally finding a silicon bug with security impacts (described later on in this post, and stay tuned for a blog from work on the bug in particular) that I had to keep quiet about until ST had a chance to review and put an advisory out, and there wasnât a whole lot I could publish about this project until then. Once that finally came out I got busy on other things.

Anyway, here we are. My long time readers will know that I like using STM32s and pairing them with FPGAs, and have got some pretty decent performance doing this, e.g. close to a Gbps of Ethernet bandwidth from the MCU to an FPGA-side RGMII MAC. Thereâs just one problem: the STM32H7 FMC needs a lot of pins - 30+ if you want all the chip selects and address lines. And theyâre not nicely located all on one side of the package either, that would be too easy. Theyâre all over the place.

Hereâs an example of what the FMC looks like on the TFBGA240 package for the H750.

And the TFBGA216 isnât any better, either.

For years, Iâve dreamed of a better way. My ultimate dream MCU, which doesnât exist because Iâm probably the only weirdo who would buy it, would be a 1 GHz Cortex-M7 or M85, probably made on TSMC 28LP, with a megabyte of NOR flash or ReRAM, a megabyte of SRAM, an RGMII MAC, multiple FPGA-style I/O banks with independent VCCIO rails, and an AXI Chip2Chip SERDES block that I could use for directly integrating with FPGA-based peripherals using only two differential pairs.

The STM32H735 paired with an external FPGA over FMC got close, but was annoying to use on a low-cost board (e.g. 4 layer batch fab) because the FMC is almost impossible to route on those constraints. Some other STM32H7 parts like the H75x line are available in an 0.8mm package which is doable (painfully) on batch fab design rules, but these have a lower max CPU speed (480 vs 550 MHz) and this is really just kicking the can down the road a bit rather than fully solving the problem. Youâre still burning a ton of pins.

A fast M7 with PCIe would almost be what I want (PCIe isnât exactly AXI, but bridging them is totally doable), but nobody makes those either. You can get Cortex-Râs with PCIe, which I seriously considered (and still want to check out) but it would still be a big jump from the familiar STM32 peripheral set. And a lot of these parts either donât have crypto acceleration or security-by-obscurity lock up the docs to the crypto accelerator, which is an absolute dealbreaker for me.

But then ST came out with the STM32MP2 line. This is a full applications processor SoC with a dual Cortex-A35, some slower auxiliary processors like an M33 and a M0+, a full GPU/NPU I may play with one day, and â most interestingly to me â a 5 Gbps SERDES with PIPE interface that could be configured to operate as either PCIe gen1/2 x1 or USB 3 depending on which internal protocol IP you connect to it (thereâs a register bit to mux them). It also kept most of the same familiar STM32 peripherals I already had lots of libraries for and experience working with, so the learning curve getting spun up on it would be short - including the same AES-GCM and TRNG IPs that I already had drivers for, and were reasonably well documented.

Itâs quite a beast with far more computing power than I needed, but I did want to have a part in my back pocket I could pull out for future designs that needed more oomph. And the PCIe would potentially allow easy memory mapping of an FPGA from firmware via only two differential pairs.

Thereâs just one problem: the STM32MP2 was clearly designed to run Linux, and the vendor BSPs included all kinds of u-boot, TrustZone, etc. stuff that I didnât care about. I just wanted a big microcontroller that could run a simple RTOS or even a while(1) { doStuff(); } event loop.

So I decided to see if I could convince the MP2 that it was, in fact, just a very fast MCU with some oddball peripherals like PCIe and LPDDR PHYs that garden-variety MCUs donât have.

I bought a STM32MP257 development board (STM32MP257F-EV1) and started out the same as I would with any other new STM32 part: added a linker script and header to stm32-cpp with the addresses of the peripherals that used the same register interface as other STM32 parts I already had supported in the library. The only difference was that the image base address was in SRAM rather than flash.

Then I built a simple LED blinky firmware for the Cortex-M33 auxiliary core and loaded it over JTAG just like I would for a regular STM32. There were a few false starts but I got a blinky running fairly quickly. Achievement #1 unlocked: I can talk to the chip and poke registers.

The next milestone was to actually boot the same blinky from flash. It took some digging through example code and wikis to figure out all of the fine points (for example, the internal SRAM is mapped at four different physical addresses with different TrustZone etc settings, but the boot ROM only lets you boot from one of them). Before too long I had a tool that took a flat binary RAM image and bolted on the necessary FSBL headers for the STM32MP2 boot ROM to load it from flash and execute. Then I made a little flasher utility that could be loaded into SRAM and would write an image from another SRAM location to flash, bootstrapping the whole process. Achievement #2 unlocked: the chip is booting from nonvolatile memory and doesnât need to be loaded over JTAG each boot.

A few things to keep in mind when preparing the FSBL image:

This firmware booted in âM33-TDâ mode, in which the boot ROM immediately transfers control to the M33 after loading the FSBL image, and the M33 has full TrustZone privileges. I chose this over âA35-TDâ (in which the A35 boots first) mostly because I wanted to do a staged bring-up of the platform and not have my first time working with the SoC also be my first time bringing up a bare metal Cortex-A.

I continued along the same way I would with any other new STM32 platform for a bit, bringing up a serial console, enabling caches, configuring the PLLs and clock tree, dumping a bunch of platform information to the console on boot, etc.

The code is all on my GitHub but a quick summary of what you need to do for bare metal bringup in M33-TD is as follows. None of the SoC setup code here requires custom assembly, it can all be done in C/C++ except for CPU configuration stuff like enabling/disabling interrupts or the FPU when youâre ready to do that.

Then it came time to get the A35 running, which I had to do before playing with the PCIe because the M33âs memory map did not allow it to talk to the PCIe BAR region â annoying, but something I could live with if the M33 is mostly acting as a management processor and all our application code is on the A35.

I had previously avoided working with Cortex-Aâs because the overhead involved in getting them set up was a lot higher.

First, once you have the A35 image in flash, you need to actually start it. Figuring this out took quite a bit of reading of various third party library code and such, the datasheet didnât make it obvious. The basic steps are:

The FSBL-A image in flash (at offset 0x0008_0000 for primary and 0x000c_0000 for fallback) itself then is launched in parallel on both cores in the cluster simultaneously in aarch64 mode (although there is a fuse you can blow to boot in aarch32 mode instead if you wanted to for some reason). The first part of this initialization does have to be done in assembly because thereâs a bunch of stuff needed that pokes hardware registers and initializes the stack etc.

Note also that this image has to be in flash: even if you have code executing on the M33 already, there does not appear to be a good way to just have the M33 dump an image into SYSRAM and have the A35 execute it: when the A35 is released to boot the ROM will check strap pins and load the image from the specified location (in my case SPI NOR flash); even though the M33 is already running the A35 is going to re-run the boot ROM.

At this point the lowest levels of the core are set up, but we donât know which core weâre on yet. So the next step is to read MPIDR_EL1 and figure out which one weâre on, since the subsequent steps vary depending on which core weâre on.

Youâll notice that I havenât said much about the DDR. Thatâs because I donât plan to use it. Itâs a Synopsys DDR3L/DDR4/LPDDR4 controller that requires a blob plus annoying PCB layout for all the data lines, uses a bunch of power, and is just all around overkill. The whole point of switching from the STM32H735 to the MP2 was to replace the parallel memory bus with PCIe and using DDR would negate most of those benefits.

Anywayâ¦ at this point, you basically have a STM32H7 on steroids:

The MP2 has the same FMC hard IP as the H735, so if I wanted to be silly I could interface it to the FPGA just like the H7. But then why go through all this trouble to bring up the more complex SoC? We want to do PCIe otherwise thereâs no point.

The STM32MP257F-EV1 has a mini PCIe slot meant for a wifi card or something, but I found some adapters to convert it to M.2. This allowed me to interface to a random old NVMe SSD for early testing, and to an M.2 FPGA module later on.

The datasheet provides some initial breadcrumbs on configuring things. We need to enable the COMBOPHY and PCIe IPs in the RCC like usual, then poke SYSCFG.COMBOPHYCR1 to specify whether weâre using the external reference clock (typically 100 MHz but the PLL can be configured for other multiplier/divide combinations) or using an internally generated clock from the RCC.

Once everything is turned on, itâs just a matter of configuring COMBOPHYCR2 to enable PCIe mode, poke COMBOPHYCR3 to calibrate the controlled impedance drivers/terminations, then wait for the other internal housekeeping to complete and the PHY to report everything is ready to go.

Finally, poke SYSCFG.PCIECR to specify the initial bus/device ID and enable the LTSSM so we can actually train the link, toggle PERST to the peripheral, and wait for SYSCFG.PCIESR1 to report successful training. Somewhat shockingly, thereâs no firmware blob or weird setup flow. It just works and trains the link with only a handful of register pokes.

Or at least, I thought it did. After some issues attempting to enumerate the bus I found it was flapping and retraining constantly.

Luckily I have a fast scope and ngscopeclient can decode PCIe and PCIe link training, so I went to work.

Looking at the startup process, everything seemed fine. The link trained up into L0 without any problems, then even passed a few TLPs before dropping into Recovery.RcvrLock, recovering for a bit, then dropping again. After that it stayed up for a while, dropped, and stayed down until the end of the waveform.

But why was it dropping? The first question was which side of the link was initiating the drop. It was pretty clear after zooming in that the STM32 was dropping (transitioning from idles in L0 to sending training sets) the first time, for no obvious reason while the link partner was still sending valid idles. So the problem was at least being detected, if not caused, on the STM32MP2.

I wondered if it might be signal integrity problems. So I fired up a quick eye pattern of both legs of the link. The RX lane (peripheral to STM32) looked fine. A bit overequalized since it was short and I was probing right at the mini-PCIe connector, but wide open with over 200 mV of eye height.

The TX (STM32 to peripheral) eye looked like nothing I had ever seen before. It was clear and wide open most of the time, but the entire eye was closed with a pretty uniform 1e-4 BER. Iâm used to seeing eyes that are squished horizontally due to jitter, vertically due to noise or reflections, etc but in such a scenario itâs usually consistent, the eye wonât have clear top and bottom bars or rising/falling edges.

The only thing I could think of was something intermittent. Maybe the signal is fine most of the time, the link comes up, then something happens - a noise burst, maybe - that blanks it out briefly before it comes back.

So I looked at the second, longer drop in the same waveform. This one was weirder: the link was fine then all of a sudden out of nowhere, the STM32MP2 started sending absolute nonsense - bit patterns that decoded as invalid scrambler values or sometimes not even well-formed 8b10b symbols at all! Then 40 Î¼s or so later the link partner noticed and went into re-training.

When I zoomed in further looking at just a few symbols on either side of the link drop, the problem immediately jumped out at me. Look at the relative phases of the purple Threshold_5 signal (a simple thresholding of the analog waveform) and the green squarewave below it (a clock recovered from the analog waveform by a DSP PLL).

At left, everything is happy. The recovered clock edges are 90Â° phased to the data allowing it to be cleanly sampled with plenty of setup and hold margin. But right about the middle of the screen, things start going sideways, literally. By the end of the D15.2 symbol the clock edge is only about 58 ps after the data edge (instead of the ideal 200ps setup/hold window for a 400ps UI at 2.5 GT/s). And by the end of the D11.7 the clock and data are on top of each other leaving no setup/hold window at all and the protocol decode starts seeing bit errors.

Both the DSP and real physical CDR PLL have limited bandwidth, so if theyâre handed this large a phase shift in <20 UI thereâs no way they will be able to keep up (although they will try).

Plotting TIE (time interval error, essentially the difference between where the CDR PLL expects a UI boundary to be compared to the actual level crossing in the real waveform) for the RX side shows pretty uniform jitter without any weird artifacts. But the TX side shows TIE jumping all over the place, railing at Â± 200 ps (half a UI - the max error possible before the edge is considered to be part of the next UI) and the CDR slewing frantically over 30 MHz above and below the nominal data rate trying and failing to stay synced.

Putting all the evidence together, itâs pretty clear that the SERDES PLL in the COMBOPHY is losing lock intermittently. Everything is fine for a while then something happens internally within the SERDES and the PLL VCO starts jumping around for a bit. This causes the transmit data to jump around (causing the link partner to fail to receive it, as seen in the scope captures) but it also will likely have similar effects on the receiver - causing the STM32 to misread incoming, well formed data as well.

Thereâs only a handful of registers for configuring the COMBOPHY PLL and everything I was writing to them looked fine according to the datasheet, so I was pretty sure it wasnât a misconfiguration. The dev board was a ST reference design which I assumed had to be fine as well.

So if itâs not hardware and itâs not software, what is it? There was really only one other thing to look at, the reference clock. I had configured the COMBOPHY to be clocked via the RCC (ck_ker_usb3pciephy, set to 25 MHz) with SYSCFG.COMBOPHYCR1 set to 0xc8 to get the 2500 MHz required VCO frequency (no spread spectrum, multiplier 100).

But the STM32MP257F-EV1 also had a dedicated 100 MHz reference clock available. Poking COMBOPHYCR1 to 0x33 to select the external clock and multiply it by 25 gave me the same 2500 MHz VCO frequency, but without the added jitter of the internal PLL (TSMC PLLTS16FFCLAFRAC2 fractional-N PLL) and RCC clock distribution network, plus perhaps the external crystal not having tight enough tolerances for this use case.

Andâ¦ it worked perfectly. The link came up, trained happily to 2.5 GT/s gen1 x1 (I figured Iâd save gen2 for later), and everything looked fine.

After this, things get a lot more tricky because the IP isnât really documented at all, at least publicly (as usual, portions of the datasheet and register map have probably appeared in various corners of the internet). Luckily I was able to find some breadcrumbs in uboot and Linux kernel code that gave me a better idea of how things are set up: the PCIe IP block has a register block on AHB5 with a standard PCIe root complex register set (these registers are mostly documented in the PCIe base spec; thereâs a bunch of vendor proprietary ones too but we donât need them to get things functional), then the actual PCIe devices are mapped into a 256 MB chunk of physical AXI address space from 0x1000_0000 to 0x1fff_ffff.

I had never worked with PCIe enumeration before so it took a bit of time to piece together the required steps. The code for this is in stm32-cpp/src/peripheral/PCIE.* and src/cpu1-a35/bsp/hwinit.cpp if you want to poke around in detail but Iâll summarize it here.

First, I read a bunch of standard registers like link status, speed, hardware IP version, etc and log them. Not strictly necessary, but helps with troubleshooting.

Thereâs a bunch of basic configuration within the standard PCIE address space that needs to be done next (after writing a magic unlock value to MISC_CONTROL_1 to remove write protection). Pick a bus number for the root complex, specify the memory limit, etc. But now we need to actually talk to the registers in the link partner. How does that work?

It turns out, the PCIe IP has an âinternal address translation unitâ (iATU) that is essentially a sort of IOMMU. It takes incoming and outgoing TLPs and translates addresses within the AXI block to PCIe BAR or configuration addresses and adds the appropriate TLP type.

So the next step is to set up a chunk of AXI space (I chose 0x1fff_0000 to 1fff_ffff, the last 64 kB of the AXI range) and configure the iATU to map this to configuration accesses to device 01:00.0 (which is the bus and device weâre going to assign to the link partner). I didnât plan to implement a full featured stack with PCIe bridges and the like, since Iâm intending to only ever be wiring the STM32 directly to an FPGA. So a lot of the configuration could be hard coded.

Then I set up a second range of AXI space (0x1000_0000 to 17ff_ffff, the first 128 MB of the AXI range) and mapped it to PCIe address 0x0000_0000. This is where weâre going to put the BAR of the link partner.

We should now have a standard PCIe configuration address block mapped at 0x1fff_0000 that we can walk and print out. I wrote some code to print out a few registers to sanity check andâ¦ got back all zeroes.

Something was clearly broken in the upper levels of the stack. The link was up, I could see DLLPs flowing and the eye was wide open. The iATU was at least configured close to valid, because I wasnât seeing any segfaults like I would if I had a completely bogus memory mapping.

I still had my probes on the PCIe signals (this testing somewhat overlapped with the clock jitter / PLL troubleshooting, but I wanted to tell the story in a more linear order to make it make sense) so the next step was to try to protocol decode some test reads and writes.

I wrote some test firmware that wrote 0xdeadbeef to the start of the configuration space, and the configuration write TLP came out of the STM32 with a valid address and an all-zero payload.

I tried writing 0xfeedface to a location in the BAR range. It also came out with the correct address and an all-zero payload.

Even more confusing, I tried readingâ¦ and the device responded! With a valid read completion TLP, and a decidedly nonzero payload. But my firmware saw the read come back as all zeroes.

So in summary: every write TLP I send to either configuration or data space has all header fields correct, but the payload is all zeroes. Every read TLP goes out normally, the device responds as it should, but my firmware sees all zeroes.

This points to something inside the STM32, either in the PCIe IP or the AXI fabric, zeroing out the data payload only without changing the address. What could possibly do this???

Looking at the STM32MP2 reference manual, there was an obvious suspect: the Resource Isolation Slave unit for Address space protection, Full (RISAF).

It sits right on the AXI bus between the PCIe and the main AXI interconnect fabric, and passes traffic through unless it sees something it doesnât like (e.g. TrustZone nonsecure domain accessing secure resource) in which case it blocks the request and fires a fault interrupt that the secure domain can handle as it sees fit.

So I threw together a quick monitor task on the M33 that polled the IASR register on RISAF5 (which is the instance protecting the PCIe AXI interface) andâ¦ sure enough, it threw a fault the moment I touched the PCIe BAR region from my firmware (which was running in EL3 secure mode since I never dropped privileges).

Just to confirm, I added a few register pokes in BSP_Init() on the M33 (the only core that is allowed to touch the RISAF configuration in M33-TD mode since itâs considered the system root of trust in that mode) that enable both privileged and unprivileged reads and writes to the entire AXI address range from the A35 in secure mode.

And everything worked perfectly. My write TLPs had the correct values as seen by the scope, and reads returned normal data to my firmware. I wrote up a basic single-device-only bus enumeration code path that dumped a bunch of information and everything worked great.

At this point, there was little doubt in my mind that I was sitting on a silicon errata that was a potential TrustZone bypass. So I poked our disclosure team at work and got the ball rolling to send an advisory out to STMicroâs PSIRT (while I found this bug in my off time, I figured it was better to have a company name and lawyers in the disclosure path in case anybody got cranky).

I wrote up an advisory and sent it off to ST, then mostly shelved things until they published something so I could talk about things in detail.

After quite some time, they published an advisory and errata, now documented as errata 2.3.33.

First: what real world deployments or use cases, if any, are potentially vulnerable? What combination of PCIe peripherals and TrustZone monitor would either not notice the issue or not react fast enough, and be possible to exploit by read side effects and/or all-zero writes, to gain privileges or escalate in some way?

Second, more interesting: is RISAF5 the only affected instance? The ST advisory and errata talks about RISAF5 but this may just be because RISAF5 is the only one that I have a working PoC for. I donât know if ST tested the others and confirmed theyâre not vulnerable to the same bug, or if nobody looked.

RISAF1 controls the backup SRAM, RISAF2 the OCTOSPI, and RISAF4 the DDR controller. There does not appear to be a RISAF3 (if it exists, itâs not mentioned in the datasheet). Writing a zero value to the right location in backup SRAM, OCTOSPI PSRAM, or external DDR is likely a much easier privilege escalation (perhaps by replacing some bytes of code or data used by the RISAF security violation exception handler itself, if this is in a cold cache line, with 0x00). If anybody is able to PoC a working exploit by this approach, and/or confirm the other RISAFs are vulnerable, I would love to see.

With PIO from the CPU, the maximum performance I was able to achieve with a software memcpy was about 1.77 Gbps (out of a theoretical peak 4 Gbps). Each strp instruction generates a TLP with 16 bytes of payload, and adding in the 20 bytes of headers + CRC we get 36 bytes of total packet size - only 44% of which is carrying useful data.

But this is already a huge boost over the FMC (which maxes out at 977 Mbps for 137.5 MHz clock and 9 bus cycles for a 64-bit APB write), to say nothing of the simplified PCB routing.

We can definitely do much better with DMA. The STM32MP2âs PCIe IP maxes out at 256 bytes per TLP (not the 4 kB max that the spec allows), which gives a 276 byte TLP and 92.75% efficiency, or ~3.71 Gbps theoretical peak. I havenât actually hit this in a benchmark but will probably try to test it at some point.

If I can get close to this, Iâll be at ~2x the throughput of PCIe PIO and ~3.8x the throughput of the FMC. Which is pretty decent.

Thereâs still a lot more work to be done. Since shelving the original testing during the disclosure window around the RISAF bug I did preliminary testing of my own home grown bare-bones PCIe stack on an Artix-7 FPGA with the STM32MP2.

I also bought an Efinix Ti375 FPGA dev board and want to try pairing its hard PCIe IP with the STM32MP2 as well. This will hopefully happen in the next few weeks and maybe turn into a blog post of its own once itâs a bit more well developed and Iâve demonstrated e.g. poking APB registers in FPGA-based peripherals from PIO code on the STM32.

Maybe if I have time Iâll try to see if I can poke the backup SRAM to 0x00 through the RISAF gate. More to come soon!

#9911. So Many AI Security Benchmarks, but None Tell the Whole Story

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Measuring artificial intelligence model security gets complex, fast, thanks to a growing patchwork of benchmarks targeting different variables in the equation. But none replace testing against your own code and workflows.

Cybersecurity firms and the makers of foundational models are improving the performance and efficiency of their artificial intelligence (AI) systems. But quantifying that performance improvement is a challenge.

While claims of more efficient models with smaller token costs arrive every week, gauging whether those models perform as well as the more general-purpose members of an AI model's family remains difficult. The lesson for organizations: Test models against your code and workflows to make the best choice for your business requirements.

National sovereign AI and cyber-defense firm Dream Group, for example, used 220,000 vulnerability records, threat intelligence reports, detection rules, and other cybersecurity documents to train an 8 billion parameter model — among the smallest modern models — to perform efficiently on cybersecurity tasks. The model — dubbed the Mid-trained Security Transformer (MiST) — improved average performance across 13 cybersecurity tasks, consisting mainly of multiple-choice and true-false questions about vulnerability analysis and cybersecurity domains.

Related:L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

The results show that stronger security capabilities do not necessarily need a more complex model; more specialized training and adding better software around the model both improve results, says Elad Ben Zaken, an AI researcher at Dream Group.

"I expect efficiency to keep improving in coding and security tasks through specialization and better workflows," he says. "The model supplies capability; the harness determines how effectively it uses context and tools. Adding more of either can increase cost without improving results."

Dream is not alone in finding ways to make models more efficient. When Anthropic released Opus 5.5 in September, for example, the company said that the model improved performance while costing 40% less than Opus 5 on "typical workloads."

However, for cybersecurity tasks, very little is typical. One model's results may mean little to companies looking for an expert system to generate secure code or to effectively find weaknesses in the enterprise's attack surface. On the offensive side, researchers are creating their own benchmarks to measure the performance of cybersecurity-focused models.

For offensive-security firm XBOW, the metrics that matter concern the ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities. Because different customers may want to use specific models, the company creates its own harness to improve outcomes regardless of the model used, says Albert Ziegler, head of AI at XBOW. While other organizations may want to use AI to analyze defensive telemetry and signals to boost detection of potential attacks, XBOW's metrics focus on finding vulnerabilities and exploit chains.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

"In its most atomic form, that's the ability of the model to find an exploit — that is our bread and butter in terms of seeing what's the value that the model produces," Ziegler says. "For other companies, this bread and butter could obviously be something else."

Anthropic's Opus 5 Thinking leads the board on one metric, correctness, among large language models. Source: Sonar's LLM Leaderboard

Another benchmark, the SEC-Bench Pro, attempts to measure an AI agent's ability to independently rediscover and trigger a known memory-safety bug in a browser engine or the Linux kernel, but only after the general location and type of bug are specified. Created by a research team at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the metric ranks Codex and GPT-5.5 as the current favorites, with an overall solve rate of 58%. It also finds that open-weight models tend to struggle, with GLM-5 only succeeding in 13 of the 344 test cases.

Other metrics measure the hacking capabilities of AI models over an entire attack chain. Government contractor Booz Allen, for example, has published its Cyber Weapons Index (CWI), which combines a model's ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities with its effectiveness at executing attacks on a target. The latest version of the list puts OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on top with a CWI of 80.5, just edging out Claude Mythos with a score of 80.

Related:Ransomware Gangs Embrace Physical Threats, Family Stalking?

"The CWI offers one empirical approach to offensive cyber capability — test models against a common enterprise network and score demonstrated actions using network evidence, rather than relying on what models say they can do," says Eric Syphard, senior vice president and head of AI at Booz Allen. "There is no single measure that captures every security risk. Evaluations need to be designed around the capability being assessed and should make their methods, environment, and success criteria clear."

Similarly, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) continues to benchmark the capabilities of AI models to complete a 32-step attack chain. So far, two models can: Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview and OpenAI GPT 5.5.

In their own research, Dream researchers found that expert curation of a primary knowledge database — a "seed corpus" — can be used to create domain-specific synthetic training data, thus avoiding relying on general knowledge databases for training specialized models. The latest MiST models, MiST-8B and MiST-30B-A3B, were evaluated using 13 different test datasets, including 1,072 multiple-choice questions about MITRE ATT&CK (SECURE-MAET) and 870 true-false questions about whether a particular piece of code is vulnerable (the PrimeVul P-C).

Overall, the various features, capabilities, and issues are hard to benchmark in any comprehensive way. While offensive security metrics and measurements of defensive capabilities are both evolving quickly, other areas — such as safety — are more difficult to benchmark. The AISI found that the most sophisticated models tend to execute unwanted actions, such as OpenAI's GPT Astra conducting unsanctioned supply chain attacks, but overall safety measurements are more anecdotal than comprehensive.

Creating a metric for a model's likelihood of taking unwanted actions, for example, is very difficult, XBOW's Ziegler says.

"Benchmarking the possibility of the model to do harm is incredibly hard," he says. "You run [the test case for the model] 1,000 times, and it doesn't do any harm, and then you run it the 1,001 time, it drops your database. That 1,001 time negates all the first thousand runs that went well."

In addition, just because a model is newer does not mean it's more secure or has more advanced security capabilities, says Joe Tyler, general manager and AI researcher at Sonar, a provider of AI code verification and governance tools. The company regularly runs the latest large language models (LLMs) through a testing pipeline to generate scores across a series of benchmarks — from cognitive complexity to vulnerability occurrence in its code — which it then posts to its LLM Leaderboard for Code Quality & Security.

The ranking can give companies a general sense of model performance, but it should only be the starting point for companies evaluating LLM security performance, Tyler says. Instead, organizations should tailor their test pipelines to their own situations.

"Start with the task and the failures you can't accept, rather than assuming the newest model is the right choice," he says. "Public benchmarks help shortlist candidates, but the decision needs evaluations that reflect your own code and workflows."

In addition, for most organizations the choice of model may be constrained by the technology platforms they've adopted. For that reason, security teams should not necessarily focus on selecting specific models but instead seek out AI-powered services that lead to more efficiency, better coverage, and faster response.

Attackers' adoption of AI means companies will need to deal with a greater influx of vulnerabilities and faster time to exploitation, says Nico Waisman, XBOW's CISO. As a result, organizations should invest in tools and processes that help security teams move faster, automate repetitive work, and reduce the time to remediation. Focus on the impact of AI-based solutions, not their raw benchmarks, he says.

"Ultimately, I wouldn't evaluate AI security tools based on which model they use or how impressive their demos look," Waisman says. "I would evaluate them based on measurable outcomes: Are they helping you identify real risks? Are they reducing your exposure? Are they making your team significantly faster? That's where the security budget should go."

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9910. 'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

The malware's focus on AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook to expose a forest of AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint.

A novel infostealer that specifically targets AI applications and development tools is changing the narrative on illicit data monetization, opening up fresh revenue streams through extortion and other abuses of the stolen data.

Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things, they said in a recent report. It targets Windows-based machines and the browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications running on them — among other apps and services — with data theft.

However, Aokigahara is notable in that it has a particular focus on emerging AI-driven assets, collecting authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools, according to Check Point. This sets it apart from many of the infostealers currently active in the wild.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

"This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software," according to Check Point.

The AI data offers unique opportunities for threat actors to benefit financially from the stealer's activities by using credentials or session tokens to "enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts," according to the report.

The malicious activity can also extend to developer and cloud environments, and thus threaten enterprises. Indeed, threat actors have already demonstrated how they use stolen credentials for GitHub accounts, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files to infiltrate cloud environments of enterprise targets.

This may also pave the way for extortion of organizations by holding stolen data for ransom, according to Check Point.

"Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services," according to the post. "If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment."

Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of security firm Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that "stolen AI credentials can yield a heavy harvest for an attacker. A paid AI subscription is a resellable asset, and the conversation history behind it is often full of proprietary code, which means these stolen sessions now carry extortion value alongside their resale value."

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

Other targeted data the malware looks for are developer and cloud credentials, including Git access data, SSH keys, and configuration files for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This data is valuable to give attackers access to private code repositories or cloud resources if the stolen credentials remain valid and have sufficient permissions, according to Check Point.

Indeed, "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring," Calderone observes, and some of those keys ultimately could give attackers access to the kingdom.

"The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run," he says.

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

Aokigahara also has built-in anti-detection mechanisms. It checks for analysis environments such as virtual machines and sandboxes, and packages stolen data into zip archives and then encrypts it before sending it to attacker-controlled servers.

Aokigahara's targeting of AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook, potentially exposing AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint. The theft of this data then opens new pathways for financial gain for attackers and thus may provide an incentive for others to do the same, according to Check Point.

This means that defenders should start treating AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, with protections comparable to those applied to cloud credentials and developer keys. To that end, security teams should hunt for AI-session theft by investigating suspicious access to local application storage and authentication-related files belonging to AI assistants, coding agents, and developer IDEs.

Organizations also should more closely protect developer and cloud credentials by reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets on endpoints, using managed identity and short-lived credentials where feasible, and restricting access to cloud resources and source-code repositories.

Further, organizations can protect assets across exposed apps and tools by revoking exposed sessions and rotating secrets. If an endpoint is suspected of compromise, according to Check Point, they should assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens, not just browser passwords.

#9909. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

The company launched the Qingyun HM650 last week and said it uses Huawei’s own Kirin X90 processor, a ten-core 20-thread machine with a clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The machine runs a newly developed enterprise version of HarmonyOS, the OS Huawei developed to end its dependence on Android and which it intends to run on most of the devices it makes.

A single Chinese government agency has reportedly signed up for 600 of the machines. That’s not an indication this machine is a curiosity, because Beijing has ordered all government entities to shift from Wintel boxes to local alternatives.

Even if Huawei is using some parts that aren’t entirely Chinese, the debut of the Qingyun HM650 is bad news for Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm, as all are suffering as the PC market shrinks due to the rising cost of memory. #9906. Introducing Project Steadfast

Recently I wrote about an idea that’s been floating around in my mind for a long time - the ability to do metaprogramming in Ruby by manipulating Ruby ASTs, similar to the macro capabilities of languages such as Lisp or Elixir. The use of eval (in its different variations) is a common metaprogramming technique in Ruby that consists of generating code at runtime from dynamically constructed strings. This is often done for performance reasons: ERB compiles templates into optimized code by generating pieces of Ruby source code then putting them together and calling eval; In Rails, the same technique is used for implementing features such as associations, or scaffolding. With eval, we can avoid paying the performance overhead that’s often associated with using DSLs in Ruby.

But using eval in a highly-dynamic context may also be error-prone, limited, and potentially vulnerable to injection attacks. Having to painstakingly construct strings containing Ruby source code can be an arduous task, especially if you want to compile a DSL into efficient code, as in the case of ERB, or my own Papercraft.

In Papercraft, HTML is generated using a DSL. Here’s an example:

While this kind of code may be used to generate HTML using the builder pattern, which is the traditional way of implementing DSLs in Ruby, it introduces a significant performance overhead. That is why in Papercraft I chose to implement a compiler that takes the code above and compiles it into the optimized form:

This does solve the performance problem (on par with ERB templates), it introduces a different problem, that complexity in the Papercraft compiler code itself. I’m not particularly proud of the Papercraft compiler code, which complexity stems from the fact that the kind of optimized code is generated dnyamically, and has to be put together from many small pieces. That’s why I’ve long been thinking about how to simplify it.

It eventually occurred to me that a tool for generating code using a general-purpose macro expansion technique, such as the quote/unquote mechanisms in languages such as Lisp or Elixir, might be a perfect fit for solving problems such as this. Such a tool may not only be used for generating new code at runtime, but can also be used for manipulating and mutating existing code at runtime.

As a very simple example of how this technique may be used, let’s implement a general-purpose validator generator. Its job is to generate a validator lambda that validates a given value against one or more conditions, which we’ll do using the === operator (this is the operator used for matching case clauses in Ruby). We can just generate a closure and iterate over the conditions:

That’s pretty nice and simple, but if we wanted to squeeze a bit more performance out of it we might want to unroll that conds.each loop, which we can do by interpolating a string containing the unrolled code, then pass it to eval:

This is perfectly doable, but notice that we have to nest the embedded code inside of the string we’re building, which is kind of unwieldy. With a quote/unquote tool, which let’s us build Ruby code out of Ruby code, we could do the following:

With #quote we’re putting code inside quotes (obviously), and with #unquote we’re temporarily escaping out of the quotes in order to perform some computation and inject the result back into the quoted code. In this case, we’re converting each of the conditions into a piece of Ruby AST by calling quote { unquote(c) === v }.

In my article Unrolled Code, I’ve explored how this technique could be applied to many different problems. Which leads us to project Steadfast.

I’m excited to announce that I’ve been selected as the recipient of a Ruby Association grant for working on developing a general-purpose macro tool for Ruby using the quote/unquote technique, with Matz as my mentor.

The scope of the project includes the development of the quote/unquote tools, as well as additional tools for generating and manipulating Prism ASTs, converting ASTs to source code, etc. The project will also explore the use of those tools in popular gems such as ERB, ActiveRecord, Roda etc. I’d like to see how far I can take those ideas, how can they be integrated into the Ruby runtime, and what are the limitations and drawbacks of this technique.

I’ll do this work in a new repository that I created called Steadfast. If you wish, you can look at some sketches I made that show possible usages for quote/unquote. Steadfast is a continuation of my work on Sirop, a tool I built for converting Prism ASTs to source code, and which is currently used by the Papercraft compiler.

Steadfast is dedicated to the courageous people of the land who persevere in the face of unimaginable violence, persecution, callousness and indifference.

Over the next four months, I’ll be sharing news of my progress on this project, which should be completed by late March 2027. I think the new techniques introduced in this project can lead to a new way of doing metaprogramming in Ruby. Hopefully, other people will find this work useful and will come up with new uses for Steadfast.

#9905. Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills

Nathan Hamiel outlines potential SecOps horror in the AI midst, as core technical capabilities go the way of reading an atlas or remembering phone numbers.

Black Hat India — Bengaluru — The use of AI as a tool to enhance cybersecurity operations is emerging as a double-edged knife for security professionals. While it can make them more capable, it could also spell the demise of the very skills they need to use it effectively.

That's the concern of Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, who has made a case for how evolving technology can erode technical skills since well before the generative AI boom. Now, that concern is getting much louder.

Speaking to Dark Reading recently, he says he began noticing the problem around 2005 and 2006, when he encountered cybersecurity professionals who lacked a firm grasp of the fundamentals of their work. At that time, he warned about the dangers of relying too heavily on various types of technical tools, declaring to cybersecurity professionals that "your tools are killing you," and warning that practitioners are moving away from being "hands-on" operators who investigate problems directly, and toward "hands-off" monitors who oversee results presented through tools, interfaces, and dashboards.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

It's a shift that's being exacerbated now by AI-driven automation, he says, and organizations need to move quickly to optimize the use of AI without the expense of cybersecurity skill-building.

While automation can simplify complex tasks and allow professionals to accomplish more, it can also distance them from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a solid understanding of the fundamentals, practitioners may struggle to recognize when a tool produces an incorrect result or when its findings require further investigation, Hamiel says.

"We need to keep these skills and not let them degrade because those skills are important to making the tools work in the best way possible," he tells Dark Reading from this week's Black Hat India conference, where he's giving a keynote entitled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems."

"What AI adds to somebody with knowledge and experience is some additional capabilities," Hamiel elaborates. "A domain expert wielding AI is going to be able to gain benefits from using that tool that a novice with no domain experience isn't going to be able to get."

This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into cybersecurity workflows. It also raises questions about how the industry will develop its next generation of experts if automation removes some of the hands-on tasks that junior professionals traditionally learn.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

The current discussion around AI often falls into extremes, Hamiel says. Some predict that the technology can go a long way toward solving major problems facing not only cybersecurity but also humanity, while others warn that it will bring the industry — and some even the world — to an end.

"You have the doomers," he says, "and you have people who say this is a big nothingburger. The truth is somewhere in the middle."

For Hamiel, understanding AI's impact requires separating what the technology can demonstrate in a controlled environment from what it can reliably accomplish in the real world. Impressive capabilities do not necessarily translate into the wholesale replacement of jobs or the disappearance of entire industries, he says.

The same distinction applies to cybersecurity, Hamiel says. Although AI can help identify vulnerabilities, generate code and support security investigations, those capabilities do not mean that the complex problems facing security teams have suddenly become easy to solve.

In fact, some recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity — such as OpenAI models autonomously hacking the Hugging Face framework, among others — may reveal a more familiar and persistent cybersecurity problem: organizations failing to address basic security weaknesses.

Related:US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

"If you read some of the incident reports, these are organizations that weren't exercising basic security hygiene," Hamiel says.

In these cases, he argues, the weaknesses were already there, waiting to be discovered. "This wasn't just low-hanging fruit; this was fruit lying on the ground where anybody who looked for it would have found it," he says.

Rather than signaling an impending cybersecurity apocalypse, such incidents could prompt what Hamiel calls a "cybersecurity correction."

"It's not that there is this huge apocalypse happening; it's that many people weren't doing the right thing for a very long time," he explains.

In other words, AI may make it easier to discover and exploit existing weaknesses, exposing the consequences of inadequate security practices. The challenge for organizations is not simply to adopt new tools but to address the underlying problems those tools bring to light.

Indeed, the potential erosion of technical skills is not a problem that began with generative AI. Hamiel sees it as part of a longer trend in which technology increasingly mediates the relationship between professionals and the problems they are responsible for solving.

Hamiel's concern reflects what is often called the irony of automation: As systems take on more responsibility, the humans overseeing them can lose opportunities to practice the skills needed when those systems fail.

The consequences could extend beyond the skills of today's practitioners to the way the cybersecurity industry develops future experts, he says, especially in how lower-level work that AI can eliminate helps helping junior professionals learn.

Tasks that might appear repetitive or straightforward can provide essential experience, allowing new practitioners to understand how systems work before progressing to more complex investigations. "If you automate that, there isn't room for them to learn," Hamiel warns.

This creates a potential long-term problem for employers. AI may allow teams to complete certain tasks more efficiently today, but organizations still need experienced professionals who can investigate unfamiliar problems, evaluate automated findings, and respond when systems behave unexpectedly.

For cybersecurity pros to use generative AI effectively, then, it's simply a matter of applying it to tasks where it offers meaningful benefits while remaining aware of the skills that might be weakened if pros rely too much on these tools to do their jobs effectively.

"The goal here is to maximize the benefits and minimize the drawbacks," Hamiel says, something that is true for the use of any technology. "That's the framing that should be placed around this," he says.

Thus, the only way that organizations can adopt AI without losing essential cybersecurity expertise is to "apply them to the right types of activities," he says.

For cybersecurity pros, this means using generative AI for tasks such as threat hunting and threat intelligence, where preliminary analysis can help professionals work through information more efficiently, Hamiel notes. AI-powered penetration-testing tools are another area of promising development, extending beyond traditional vulnerability scanning to perform more complex tasks, he says.

Ultimately, the question is not whether AI will change cybersecurity, Hamiel says. That genie is most certainly already out of that bottle. Ultimately, the real challenge is ensuring that the industry does not become so dependent on increasingly capable tools that it loses the human expertise required to use them effectively, he says.

"Skills and expertise make your AI use more effective," Hamiel concludes. "If you have two professionals, and both use AI, the one with more knowledge of the task is going to make better use of the AI."

#9904. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#9903. SBOMs Alone Can't Reveal the Scope of a Supply Chain Attack

A recent Shai-Hulud attack shows defenders need real-time visibility into production code and affected services to respond to supply chain compromises.

ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — Depending on a software bill of materials (SBOM) to determine what happens when a malicious package slips past security checks can leave defenders struggling to establish what code actually executed, which systems it touched, and how far the compromise spread.

In a session at the ISC2 Security Congress 2026 this week, Atlassian product security manager Deepam Kanjani used a real-world compromise involving the Shai-Hulud worm to highlight incident response challenges, including gaps in runtime visibility, transitive dependency ownership, and attacker attribution.

In the session, Kanjani said he had altered all identifying details, figures, and the sequence of events to protect confidentiality, though his first-person, war-room narrative of underlying attack techniques, technical behaviors, and challenges was based on real events at a large-scale software-as-a-service (SaaS) environment.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

Kanjani described the incident as involving a package that appeared legitimate, with a matching SHA hash, more than 3,400 GitHub stars, and a repository that looked credible to the company's security tooling. But hidden three layers deep in the package was a malicious transitive dependency named shai-hulud, after the giant sandworms in the Dune movie series. Because it was not a direct dependency, it did not surface in a top-level dependency audit.

The first inkling that something was wrong came when a behavioral scanner flagged the package as running something it shouldn't have been running. Incident responders initially dismissed the alert as a likely false positive because the hash matched and there was no other obvious indication of the package being malicious.

Additionally, the SBOM reported the environment as clean when the security team consulted it. What they did not realize at the time was that the SBOM was two development sprints out of date, Kanjani said.

As the response unfolded, the team could not say with confidence which services used the package. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided initial clues but could not establish which services were affected or how far the compromise had spread. Responders needed runtime evidence to determine what code had actually executed and what it could access.

Without that runtime telemetry, they had to correlate logs manually across more than 400 services, leaving them without a reliable picture of the compromise's potential reach. An initial Slack message from the incident response handler to enterprise stakeholders made matters worse by being too vague and prompting a set of parallel investigations into the still-unfolding event.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

The security team's efforts to identify the attacker by tracing registry ownership, npm maintainer history, publisher identities, and GitHub records quickly led them to dead ends. The repository had been copied from a legitimate project, and the publisher's identity and account history appeared to have been fabricated, Kanjani said.

Researchers have subsequently attributed at least some of the later Shai-Hulud attacks to a threat actor tracked as TeamPCP.

The key takeaway, according to Kanjani, is that organizations need to look beyond SBOMs and dependency inventories and instead base incident response around what actually runs in production. The focus should be to equip security teams to identify, scope, prioritize, and contain incidents and enable real-time visibility into affected services and the potential scope of a compromise.

"You are triaging a runtime graph. Not a dependency file. Your tools must reflect that," he said.

Kanjani recommended that organizations keep deployed SBOMs under 72 hours old and try to ensure that more than 98% of production services meet that threshold. He also recommended enabling runtime capabilities to detect unknown module loads in under 90 seconds and daily registry checks to detect lookalikes of internal package names within 24 hours of publication.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Kanjani described these as targets that organizations should calibrate for their own environments rather than as universal benchmarks. In addition, security teams should focus on the operation rather than the operator, Kanjani said. "Identity signals rotate. Operational necessities don't. Build detection around what the worm must do to function — not who's driving it."

All communications with stakeholders regarding a security incident also need to be direct and unambiguous. The key is to be honest, he said, while making sure to present the details in language appropriate for the intended audience.

"Don't bullsh-t. Tell them the reality in a way they can absorb it," he said. "You don't want to sell panic."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.
