#9890. I’m not a fan of Deno’s security model (2024)

this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts so I can get it out of my head and move on. weâre gonna talk about how Deno approaches security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach is fundamentally insecure and misleading.

Deno is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager, a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff thatâs not important for our story. itâs not a JavaScript implementation, so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that.

one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system (itâs under the âSecure by defaultâ header on their landing page). the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world, Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run

the standard library will only allow code.ts to read /tmp/dir and run uname.

additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like

will display a nice little prompt in the terminal:

(aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs potential access to any website, it needs to request actual access to all the websites, which is less than ideal)

if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system.

of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one. weâll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read about this.

(if youâre only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the next section).

so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. itâs not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything, itâs just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do.

you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin. as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. itâs usually okay, because terminals wonât, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, youâre supposed to be able to freely cat files without risking arbitrary code execution. itâs markedly less okay if you allow malicious code to do whatever with the terminal and then print a prompt on the same exact terminal.

you could, like, hide the prompt by messing with terminal colors. (this one got closed in 2026 because the permission prompt is âpartially visibleâ (you can see an emoji) and âAI agents tend toâ change terminal colors, so thatâs a âvalid use-caseâ)

or trick the user into pre-feeding approval into stdin.

or trick the terminal into feeding approval into stdin as a response to some request. (terminal wonât ever send Enter to stdin to avoid executing commands, but âpress Enter to continueâ is common enough to not be suspicious; the user never sees the actual prompt). hereâs an asciicast of that, I think it looks quite cool.

the specific issue on the screencast is long patched; the issue with terminal colors is not. that doesnât really matter because the real issue is using an attacker-controlled channel for security-sensitive information. itâs like executing attacker-controlled JS code on a webpage and then asking for password on the same page. you canât know that the page is in a safe state, so you canât trust any input.

even if Deno manages to patch every single issue with the âstandardâ escape codes, you never know which non-standard codes even exist out there. many terminals have some, itâs impossible to predict how they will interact with your prompt.

(aside: how come sudo can do it then? the difference is that sudo asks for the password first, before running any other code. to trick sudo that way youâd need to fuck up terminal state before you even type sudo, and do it quietly enough that you donât notice it while you type it. if some terminal allows it, Iâd consider it a bug in the terminal)

so, thereâs a weird thing with this command I wrote above (Iâll copy it here for reference):

what does --allow-run=uname even mean? itâs not like programs have canonical names, itâs not org.gnu.coreutils.uname, itâs not even /nix/store/8k1dmzr3gwzqdgw45nzj76902ca7g1is-coreutils-full-9.5/bin/uname. itâs just a shortcut for âlook at all the directories in PATH one-by-one to see if you can find uname thereâ.

you can set environment variables for the child process without needing any extra permissions, so what if we just

once again, we have a pretty and convenient interface that doesnât really make sense from the security standpoint. it would be nice if programs were uniquely identified by their names, but theyâre not, and pretending they are leads to security holes.

funnily enough, I didnât even think that this issue would be there when I poked at Deno for the first time, so I havenât reported it until now (spoiler alert: this is a comment on a GitHub issue that I created for the problem Iâll explain below).

so letâs imagine we fixed that. itâs not that hard, we can force PATH to be whatever it was when the runtime started, or always require fully-qualified paths, or prompt with a fully-qualified path before running. are we safe now?

lol no of course weâre not. while PATH decides which executable gets run, dynamically-linked executables (so, like, most executables) require dynamic loader to actually start. dynamic loader is a program that, well, loads the executable into memory, finds its dependencies and does a bunch of other fun stuff we wonât get into. the important part is that dynamic loader is configurable via environment variables. you can probably see where this is going now.

LD_PRELOAD instructs the dynamic loader to load specific dynamic library when loading executables. dynamic libraries can execute arbitrary code on load. we can just pass LD_PRELOAD and weâve completely escaped the sandbox once again:

I reported this some time ago and now they patched it by disallowing to set environment variables starting with LD_. this, once again, fixes a specific issue while ignoring the larger problem: âpermission to run a single commandâ is mostly not a useful concept. (you can do secure interfaces by allowing to run a single command, like git-over-SSH does, but generally both the environment and the command need to be prepared to handle it)

say, for example, our script wants to invoke the $EDITOR so user can edit some data (think git commit messages). thatâs a very natural permission request, and itâs also an unmitigated disaster because most editors are configurable enough for running one to be a full sandbox escape. itâs easy for user to absent-mindedly grant --allow-run=vim (âwell, sure, I want to edit this file!â), but then the script can just set VIMINIT='!rm -rf /*' and oops, all my files are gone. most programs are configurable, often in some ways you wonât think about (like LD_PRELOAD), and attacker controls the execution enviornment. âpatch some specific ways to configure programsâ is not the solution, the solution is to sandbox all the code, not just JS code.

when we discussed all this stuff in GitHub issues, a Deno developer wrote:

The main thing it protects you against is malicious code that isn't smart enough.

deno tries really hard to do what the operating system should be doing. it emulates syscall filtering by filtering standard library calls. unfortunately, this breaks down the second you need to run code that doesnât use Deno standard library. it also uses somewhat flawed approach to permission management that looks good (wow, runtime prompts! omg, I can just --allow-run=uname!), but introduces security risks. in doing this, it implicitly requires user to understand all the implications of various permissions and their combinations, which can be really hard.

Deno process is not actually sandboxed, it only pretends it is. I didnât mention some more boring issues like âDeno doesnât prevent you from following symlinks that lead outside of the sandboxâ because they all just boil down to this simple one: the process is not sandboxed.

one can argue that this pseudo-sandboxing is better than nothing: after all, not all the malicious code is smart enough. I disagree: Deno permissions give a false sense of security and can lure someone into running untrusted code without proper sandboxing.

itâs possible that you can use Deno sandboxing safely if you:

in particular, you may be safe if youâre running untrusted code with no permissions at all in a non-interactive context and use some other mechanism to control resource consumption.

I still donât think you should do it. this path is riddled with footguns because youâre executing untrusted code in a fully-privileged process, and the moment you need some OS interactions youâre no longer running code âwith no permissions at allâ. you should not try to figure out which stdlib APIs can lead to a sandbox escape when combined. you should just use a proper sandbox.

Iâm not a fan of Denoâs security model.

also, please: donât harass Deno developers. we have a technical disagreement, but no technical disagreement was ever solved by harassment. this post is explicitly not an invitation to do it. Iâve already explained my point of view to them, they disagreed, and thatâs okay. you donât need to reiterate it, it wonât help anybody.

#9889. AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Artificial intelligence is everywhere in healthcare, from doctors' intake forms to cancer screenings. But in some cases, life-and-death uses are outpacing cybersecurity.

Patients walk into a doctor's office and are swiftly asked permission for artificial intelligence (AI) scribes to document notes full of sensitive health information. That intake conversation is just one entry point, now that AI is embedded throughout the patient life cycle and accessing more data than most organizations can secure.

This raises significant concerns for a sector that historically struggles to secure legacy equipment and highly sought-after data, even before AI was added to the mix. Advancements could save invaluable time during patient care, but security will present hurdles in the form of supply chain risks that stem from AI vendor compromise, data leakage through prompts, and AI-generated social engineering campaigns.

A recent Proofpoint report, "2026 Study on Cybersecurity in Healthcare," notes that "AI adoption is accelerating faster than governance." Forty-five percent of organizations confirmed they had embedded AI into their systems, but 60% lacked the necessary controls to govern that sensitive data.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Healthcare organizations are rapidly deploying AI to record intake conversations, and customer conversations increasingly revolve around how physicians are using AI for clinical decisions and, more importantly, how they are protecting those tools, says Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint. Some Proofpoint customers use the OpenEvidence open source AI tool for research and diagnosis because it can integrate with Epic Systems, a widely used platform for electronic health records (EHR).

"The challenge is making sure physicians aren't putting sensitive information into that tool, so it does get challenging," Biddle tells Dark Reading.

Even seemingly generic details, like a patient's eye color, combined with a specific injury, like a left tibia fracture, could qualify as protected health information (PHI). That makes data sensitivity a major concern when feeding information into AI tools. Therefore, organizations should focus on securing the underlying data rather than the tool itself, Biddle says.

AI's use is spreading fast, which complicates how organizations think about risk. Tony Sabaj, head of Americas channel SEs at Check Point, says AI's pattern-recognition capability is already improving clinical care, catching early signs in cancer screenings, triaging critical patients, and reviewing electrocardiograms to "generate reports faster and with more accuracy."

Beyond the clinic, health insurers are using AI for claims processing and fraud detection; like other industries, healthcare is also building digital twins to model operational scenarios at scale.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Some of AI's most visible momentum is in reducing administrative burdens, including documentation that converts clinician-patient conversations into draft notes, scheduling, intake, coding, and patient communications, says Cindi Carter, global chief information security officer at Check Point. It's also being used behind the scenes to support operational planning, research, and cybersecurity, she adds.

Organizations often sort AI tools into "medical" or "administrative" buckets. The first consists of diagnostic AI or treatment recommendation systems, while the latter includes intake forms or scheduling. Carter is concerned that these labels may undermine the downstream risks that administrative tools can still pose because a "documentation tool can still influence what becomes part of the medical record" and lead to clinical consequences.

In pharmaceutical and precision medicine, AI investment is outpacing security investment, Sabaj says. And as AI reaches further into healthcare, organizations need to make sure that existing regulatory frameworks keep pace. Guardrails often center on protecting data leakage, but safeguards should also ensure that if AI is taking any kind of medical action, it's limited to known parameters, he says.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

"We continue to see breaches of medical information, and AI has the potential to exacerbate this issue," Sabaj tells Dark Reading.

To get ahead of the threat, some hospitals are building their own AI tools, using open weight models and training large language models on proprietary data, rather than relying on public platforms to handle sensitive PHI.

Carter's concerns extend beyond confidentiality. Despite progress, AI is known to hallucinate. What if AI produces an inaccurate summary, omits an important detail, or acts on manipulated information? The organization can lose confidence in the information supporting care without a record ever being stolen, she says.

The CISO question then becomes broader, she says, shifting from "What data left?" to "What can this system see, what can it change, and can we reconstruct what happened?"

"In healthcare, we are protecting sensitive information and the integrity of decisions that depend on it," Sabaj says.

In the relatively short time span since rapid AI adoption took off, Phil Englert, VP of medical device security at Health-ISAC, says he has already observed changes that will affect how much sensitive data floods systems. As AI becomes increasingly integrated, when a cyber incident occurs, organizations frequently lose patient identifiers, medical records, insurance details, and other clinical or financial data — all considered PHI.

Englert cites recent Health and Human Services data that shows hacking and other IT-related incidents continue to be the leading causes of major healthcare breaches. Denver Health Medical Plan reported a breach Oct. 1 that affected 238,083 individuals, triggered by an exposed vendor access key through AI platform SquareML.

This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings, which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that an organization's security posture is often only as strong as that of its partners."

While organizations need to secure AI within their own environments, they also need to protect themselves as threat actors use it to craft more convincing and effective social engineering attacks, Englert warns. Healthcare organizations are seeing increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, deepfakes, voice impersonation attacks, and QR-code phishing — any method to exploit human trust in a sector driven by speed and precision.

While healthcare organizations can't seem to shake the ransomware threat, which "remains one of the most damaging facing the sector," AI-enabled attacks are a top cybersecurity concern for 2026, he adds.

Implementing effective guardrails has proved significantly challenging. Carter offers five recommendations informed by the governance and life cycle risk themes in the Joint Commissions and the Coalition for AI Health guidance: visibility, boundaries around data and actions, evidence from vendors, validation and meaningful human oversight, and continuous monitoring.

Organizations should maintain AI inventory and give staff a straightforward way to disclose unsanctioned uses as shadow AI risks pummel the sector. Limiting what data AI can handle is also essential; Carter recommends that access to information should not automatically confer authority to update records, send communications, or initiate transactions.

"AI compresses the time between a mistake and material loss," Carter says, and that should be reflected in organizations' safeguards.

Implementation also depends on organizational maturity. While talking with security officers across the industry, Proofpoint's Biddle has observed varying levels of AI adoption. Some are quite far in the process, while others are still cautious and taking it slow, she says, noting that healthcare tends to lag behind other industries when it comes to technology.

Many organizations lack resources but continually face disruptive attacks that severely affect patient care.

"It doesn't seem to be getting any better, unfortunately," Biddle says.

Getting better requires money, but when CISOs stand in front of the board and request investments to shore up defenses, they are often hit with: "Why do you need to spend this amount?" says Biddle. It's difficult because they are competing with budget dollars for life-saving devices, she says.

"But I would say: Leverage the impact of cyber safety," Biddle adds. "Cyber safety is patient safety."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Actions Lockfiles Reach GA to Secure Workflow Dependencies

Nov 06, 2026 3 min read

GitHub has made workflow dependency lockfiles for GitHub Actions generally available on October 28, 2026, two weeks after the feature entered public preview. Workflows can maintain clear tag and branch references. The runner executes the specific commits listed in the .github/workflows/actions.lock file, even if those references change later. The feature is available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. The GA release includes the capabilities from the preview.

The change targets a long-standing weakness in how Actions resolves dependencies. A reference like actions/checkout@v4 or a branch name can change. This means a hacked action can add bad code to a pipeline without altering the repository using it. Teams can pin to full commit SHAs, but this reduces readability. It also leaves transitive dependencies, like those from composite actions, unpinned. Lockfiles address both gaps by recording commits for direct and transitive dependencies.

Tooling comes through the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI, hosted in the gh-actions-lock repository, which generates and maintains the lockfile. Adoption follows the workflow. Once a workflow is onboarded, every dependency needs a lockfile entry. The Actions runtime then runs the recorded commit, no matter where the tag or branch points. This lets teams migrate incrementally rather than converting an entire organization at once. The extension has a verification mode. It checks if the lockfile is up to date without changing any files. This way, it can act as a CI gate to spot differences between workflow files and the lockfile.

Dependabot integration addresses the usual cost of pinning, which is stale pins. When Dependabot opens a version update for an action in an onboarded workflow, it also updates the matching lockfile entry. Both changes appear in the same pull request, so the workflow reference and locked commit stay in sync. GitHub says this works without additional configuration. For governance, enterprise, organization, and repository admins can enable a "Require lockfile" policy. This policy helps enforce adoption at the relevant scope.

GitHub is explicit about the limits of the mechanism. A lockfile guarantees that runs use the commits you locked, but it does not determine whether those commits are safe, and the announcement advises reviewing dependencies before locking them. The security value therefore depends on the review that happens when an entry is created or updated. In practice, the Dependabot pull request becomes the review point, and teams that auto-merge those updates will carry any malicious change straight into the lockfile.

The release arrives as GitHub tightens other Actions defaults. A November 2 changelog entry announced that pull_request_target will be blocked by default starting December 2, another change aimed at limiting how untrusted code reaches privileged workflow contexts.

For teams evaluating adoption, setup instructions are in the GitHub Docs page on workflow dependency lockfiles. A reasonable starting point is to onboard a few high-privilege workflows, such as release or deployment pipelines, add the staleness check to CI, and confirm that Dependabot's combined pull requests fit existing review practices before enabling the enterprise-wide policy.

Competing platforms have not announced a native equivalent so far. GitLab's pipeline security guidance advises users to manually pin includes and components to commit SHAs. Users should also pin images to digests. After the March 2026 supply chain incidents, GitLab introduced open-source pipeline execution policies. These policies focus on blocking known attack patterns instead of creating a dependency manifest. Microsoft's Zero Trust guidance for Azure Pipelines also suggests using SHA pinning. It advises limiting Marketplace extensions too.

CircleCI orbs use a central semantic-versioning registry instead of commit hashes. This approach keeps the registry immutable. Teams on these platforms often use cross-platform tools. For example, they might use pinner to pin tags to SHAs and add a CI verification step. They may also rely on scanners like ActionSieve to flag unpinned references.

These tools pin the reference written in the pipeline file but do not resolve transitive dependencies, which is the gap GitHub's lockfile design addresses. As with GitHub's feature, none of them judges whether a pinned dependency is trustworthy, so the review step that precedes locking remains the control that matters.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9886. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#9885. GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The supply chain attack campaign's shift toward developer endpoints and cloud access signals what could be next for the cybercrime outfit.

A new wave of GhostAction attacks has largely failed, but this supply chain campaign operator is well-positioned to cause more chaos down the line.

GhostAction, an ongoing campaign in which attackers target GitHub by compromising developer accounts and injecting GitHub Actions workflow files into repositories.

Workflows tell GitHub Actions what code to execute when events occur (such as when a commit is pushed or a pull request is opened); these malicious workflows rely on GitHub's high trust in these files (by design), seizing repository secrets, package publishing tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, credentials embedded in source code, and much more.

The idea is that an initial compromise could be leveraged into more compromises and access points across repositories, CI/CD systems, and cloud environments, not unlike many supply chain worms observed in the wild lately, albeit functioning differently.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations. What has changed is an apparent escalation of the technique beginning this month. During an earlier Oct. 8-12 wave, attackers pushed the security-audit.yml workflow into roughly 30,000 repositories, using compromised accounts to distribute credential-stealing code at scale. But GitGuardian on Oct. 27 published research highlighting further escalation. GitGuardian's Gaetan Ferry wrote that between Oct. 13 and 21, GhostAction's operator "pushed 72,000 commits to 23,000 public repositories," noting that 8,000 of them were new targets.

During this latest wave of the campaign, GitGuardian observed that once a developer account is compromised, the operator would deploy different payloads depending on which runner the repositories were hosted on. Runners are the systems that execute GitHub Actions workflows. Many organizations use GitHub-hosted runners, while others configure self-hosted runners that run inside their own environments.

These payloads include one called "seven workflows," which searches GitHub runner repositories and wikis for credentials including AI-provider API keys; the "Security-audit.yml" file seen in earlier GhostAction attacks that searches GitHub-hosted source code and Git history for credentials; self-hosted runner payloads targeting self-hosted CI runners; a payload targeting GitHub runners and AWS-requesting GitHub OIDC tokens (in order to assume AWS roles and achieve cloud account access); and the font stealer payload, which is the most notable workflow payload seen in recent attacks, due to its provenance.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

The font stealer family installs a Node.js credential stealer on local developer machines, disguised as a VS Code task. The technique appears to be copied from PolinRider, a campaign that hides obfuscated loaders in developer repositories to steal credentials and has been associated with North Korea. The attacker also added PolinRider loaders between Oct. 22 and 26 to repositories already impacted by GhostAction. Ferry says that out of the five payloads, only the PolinRider-styled local stealer had a chance to successfully run, but GitGuardian has no evidence that any run actually occurred.

GitGuardian could not assess whether there was overlap between GhostAction and PolinRider, but hypothesized that GhostAction's operator possibly copied a public PolinRider launcher in order to target an overlapping set of victims.

Jenn Gile, cofounder of OpenSourceMalware (which previously covered the GhostAction attacks this month and detected signs of the PolinRider copycat a few weeks ago), tells Dark Reading that the PolinRider clone illustrates some of the inner workings of the GhostAction group.

"What we're seeing looks like imitation, not evolution. The fake-font technique in GhostAction is a copy of what DPRK's PolinRider campaign has been using nearly all of 2026," she says in an email. "The multiple payloads are real, but they're variations on a theme (five workflow versions over about ten days in one repo we examined), not a new capability. Historically, we might have called this evolution because it took real skill to figure out. But this looks a lot like an LLM helping the threat actor test different variants."

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

All of that said, GitHub identified and prevented execution of the malicious workflows, GitGuardian noted. However, importantly, the attackers still demonstrated persistent access to nearly 1,800 compromised accounts, many of which had already been used in earlier GhostAction activity; "1,382 of the 1,792 compromised accounts had already been used on Oct. 8, so the same stolen tokens keep working," according to Ferry.

Ferry tells Dark Reading that the campaign has been "highly ineffective on the malicious workflows side." But even if there's no sign this wave succeeded, the nature of the payloads (such as the one aimed at gaining cloud access) also shows where the attackers may intend to pivot next, toward internal networks where there are fewer platform-level protections that could thwart their efforts.

"We expect new waves to appear in the near future, with revised payloads," he explains. "This 'fail early and adapt fast' strategy has already been observed for this threat actor."

Given that targeted accounts or repositories remain compromised, repo owners should look for and delete the files that GitGuardian lists in the IoC section of the blog, on every branch. And, if signs of compromise are detected, users should revoke the account's tokens across the board and rotate every credential committed in the affected repository or its history, as well as every Actions secret and wiki credential.

#9884. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

The KDE Project announced, in 2025, that Plasma 6.7 would be the last version of the desktop environment that would support X11 sessions. Those who keep up with KDE's announcements no doubt expected it when Plasma 6.8 dropped X11 support as promised. What seems to have come as a surprise, at least to a number of Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop users, is that the Fedora 44 release—which shipped in April with Plasma 6.6—received an update to Plasma 6.8 that swept away the X11 session without much warning. Despite the surprise, it is gone for good: the Fedora Engineering Steering Committee (FESCo) has voted against a request to revert the update for Fedora 44 and the just-released Fedora 45.

#9882. Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Researchers can't quite explain why cyber threats look so different in Italy compared with everywhere else.

To read this article in Italian, click here!

Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

InfoQ Homepage News Vault Fork OpenBao Adds External Keys and Quantum-Ready TLS

Nov 06, 2026 4 min read

OpenBao has released version 2.7, adding read scaling for PostgreSQL-backed deployments, support for external hardware security module (HSM) and key management service (KMS) keys, and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. The release also introduces control groups for human review of sensitive operations and new headers intended to keep requests consistent across load-balanced OpenBao nodes.

OpenBao began as a community fork of HashiCorp Vault after HashiCorp changed Vault's licence from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License in 2023. The project is now governed under the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation and is distributed under MPL 2.0, an Open Source Initiative-approved licence. Its stated aim is to provide a secrets manager under open governance rather than control by a single vendor.

The fork was both ideological and commercial. Some users objected to the loss of an OSI-approved licence and to the possibility that a vendor could change the terms governing infrastructure they had already adopted. Others saw a practical opportunity: Vault had placed capabilities such as namespaces, HSM integration and advanced scalability behind enterprise licences, while an open fork could make comparable functionality available without those restrictions. The move followed the wider pattern that produced OpenTofu from Terraform and Valkey from Redis.

OpenBao has developed well beyond a simple continuation of Vault Community Edition. Since the fork, the project has added namespaces for multi-tenant isolation, plugin-based auto-unseal integrations, and read scalability for its integrated Raft storage backend. Version 2.7 extends that scaling work to PostgreSQL, allowing standby OpenBao instances using that backend to serve reads in a similar way to Raft-based deployments.

Alex Scheel announced the release for the OpenBao project, writing that it adds "PostgreSQL horizontal scalability, External HSM and KMS-Backed Keys support, and Post-Quantum Cryptography". He also noted that the release arrived after a shorter development cycle than the previous one and included "many substantial features and several major security patches".

The external keys feature lets the PKI and Transit secrets engines use key material held in an HSM or KMS rather than storing it inside OpenBao. Support is delivered through third-party plugins, building on the auto-unseal plugin work in the previous release. This should appeal to organisations that must keep root certification authority keys or other high-value material under hardware control.

The post-quantum work adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM to TLS listeners, certificate authentication, PKI and Transit. Operators can therefore use post-quantum signatures and key exchange in relevant parts of the platform. The change does not by itself make a deployment quantum-safe: clients, certificate authorities and surrounding systems must also support the chosen algorithms. It does, however, give OpenBao users a route to begin testing hybrid and post-quantum configurations.

Control groups add an approval workflow to OpenBao. A new control_group stanza in an ACL policy can require a second party to review access to specified paths. This is aimed at high-risk operations where a single authenticated identity should not be able to act alone.

The release also includes breaking changes. The separate HSM distribution has been discontinued because the PKCS#11 plugin is now externalised. Vendor-specific built-in auto-unseal mechanisms for Alibaba Cloud, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud have also moved to plugins. Kerberos, LDAP and RADIUS authentication, along with the LDAP secrets engine, have moved into the openbao-plugins repository. The file storage backend has been removed; the project had never recommended it for production because it lacks high availability and transactions.

Luca Berton, who interviewed Scheel at Open Source Summit Europe, wrote that external keys allow operators to "run your PKI root backed by an HSM" with key material comparable to Vault Enterprise managed keys. He also highlighted the importance of post-quantum support before government transitions expected around 2030, citing the risk that encrypted traffic recorded today could be decrypted in the future.

Commercial support is also becoming part of the OpenBao ecosystem. ControlPlane launched ControlPlane Enterprise for OpenBao in March, offering security hardening, supply-chain assurance, rapid CVE remediation, optional FIPS 140-3 compliance support and 24/7 technical support. That offering illustrates how an open-source project can remain freely licensed while vendors compete on operational assurance. ControlPlane positions the product as a supported path for organisations that want OpenBao's licence and governance model but still need enterprise-style operational commitments. Its materials also contrast OpenBao's MPL 2.0 licence with Vault's BSL 1.1 licence and note that OpenBao retains API compatibility with Vault for many use cases.

Secrets management being a foundational dependency has been covered in InfoQ recently. We previously reported on Vault 2.0 and IBM's support model following its acquisition of HashiCorp, as well as on the broader pattern of community forks preserving open standards after vendor licence changes. OpenBao's progress suggests that the fork is becoming a credible alternative rather than merely a protest project.

OpenBao version 2.8 is expected to focus more on security and stability, with likely improvements to authentication. For teams evaluating a migration, the immediate questions are less about individual features than about operational maturity: plugin lifecycle management, PostgreSQL high-availability configuration, post-quantum client compatibility and the availability of support for production incidents.

#9880. Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

The enigmatic service is providing popular AI coding tools to mainland China and other regions where OpenAI and Anthropic products are not officially for sale — but with key security features turned off.

A mysterious relay service is installing authentic but unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools for enterprise users overseas, and making dangerous configuration changes that put those organizations at risk.

The AI relay, first spotted by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, appears to be designed to bypass regional restrictions that prevent certain countries and regions from using AI tools and platforms of US companies. According to Symantec's report published Thursday, the relay service installs genuine versions of the command-line interfaces (CLIs) for Codex and Claude Code on enterprise systems, but reconfigures them to route requests through the relay's infrastructure rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's networks.

On the surface, this appears to be the case of a gray market provider or unauthorized reseller providing the AI tools to markets where they are not officially sold. Symantec researchers noted that the service, which has been active since early 2026, has installed the tools on systems at a dozen organizations, primarily in mainland China but also in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

But the relay service also disables security safeguards for the tools, and the research team said it's unclear why it's being done (no malware or malicious activity has been observed thus far). One thing is for certain, according to Symantec: the relay service is creating enormous cyber-risk for the organizations using it.

Brigid O Gorman, senior intelligence analyst at the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading that researchers found a suspicious PowerShell downloader that they later determined to be "an AI-agent hijack script." After investigating further, the team found similar activity on other networks and traced it to the unauthorized relay service.

According to Symantec's report, when a user of the AI relay installs a legitimate Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, the fileless PowerShell or bash script is fetched from "a lookalike domain by a one-line command that the user appears to run themselves. While this evokes the specter of attack techniques like ClickFix and InstallFix, the research team noted that the CLI clients aren't modified or Trojanized in any way.

And yet, the tools perform suspicious actions that heighten risks for enterprises. For example, the reconfigurations turn off the CLIs' execution sandbox, which is a key security feature because it limits what the AI coding tools can do.

Related:F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud

Additionally, the relay service enables network access for the write sandbox, turns off telemetry and error reporting features, and replaces the user's API credentials with relay-issued tokens. In one case observed by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, the script logged a user out of their Anthropic session and deleted their authentication variables before reissuing credentials controlled by the relay service.

"Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot," the report stated.

The relay service activity is something of an enigma. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team said it's unclear why the operators of the client-side relay would need this level of control over users' systems, though the researchers did not observe any evidence of the operators abusing the access. The report noted that the architecture of the service would support malicious exploitation of the access if the operator's intentions were to change.

Furthermore, the Claude Code keys issued by the relay service are formatted with the prefix that Anthropic reserves for subscription-based OAuth tokens, "which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers," the team wrote.

Related:AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too

On the other hand, disabling security features hints at a potential fraud operation involving stolen credentials or payment cards, or even the malicious resale of prompts and files that run through the relay infrastructure. Gorman says it's "certainly notable" that the relay disables execution sandboxes and establishes its own persistent credentials.

"We did not see any malicious activity being carried out using these relay services, so any commentary on the potential intended goals of those using it are speculative," Gorman says. "However, a relay in this position can see every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account."

Symantec provided indicators of compromise (IoCs) in the report, even though technically speaking there have been no compromises at this stage. "The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted," the report stated.

Nevertheless, the research team warned that using the service presents serious risk to corporate networks. And while the relay appears to be aimed at regions where Codex and Claude Code tools aren't officially offered, organizations looking for cheaper alternatives and users engaging in shadow AI activity could potentially find their way to such a service.

Prior to becoming a technology journalist in 2000, he worked as a weekly and daily newspaper reporter in Virginia, where he won three Virginia Press Association awards in 1998 and 1999. At TechTarget and Dark Reading, he has won several Azbee awards, including the 2026 National Silver Award for a series on vibe coding.

At Dark Reading, Rob currently covers security operations, cloud security, and Internet infrastructure. He has a keen interest in malvertising activity and the certificate authority industry, and has written extensively on both topics. He graduated from the University of Richmond in 1997 with a degree in journalism and English. A native of Massachusetts, he lives in the Boston area.

#9879. Nspawn 3.0: A Docker-compatible Engine API for systemd-nspawn containers

Everything you need to know about systemd-nspawn.

2.0.0 gave the machines that mount docker’s socket a read-only Docker API, enough for Traefik or Dozzle to find them. 3.0.0 serves the API with its changes, on the host too. In between:

The host’s socket is /run/nspawn/api.sock, opened by nspawn-api.socket. Its main purpose is compatibility: tools that manage containers through the Docker API, like GitLab Runner’s docker executor, can use nspawn’s machines instead. nspawn is still the command line for managing them, but the docker command works against the socket too.

The packages ship the socket turned off. Once it listens, nspawn-api.service starts on the first connection:

With DOCKER_HOST pointing at it, the docker command talks to nspawn:

The API server is a client of the bus service, as the command line is. Everything it does is a method of org.nspawn, under the same polkit actions: reads and waits need org.nspawn.inspect, logs and changes need org.nspawn.manage. Every user can connect, but polkit is never asked to prompt, since nothing on a socket can answer an authentication agent. Root can do everything, and any other user needs a polkit rule, like nspawn-wheel.rules, which the packages ship as an example. As with the docker group, a user with org.nspawn.manage is root on the host: a machine runs commands as root and can mount any host path.

What one socket’s clients hold at once (connections, log and event streams, waits, attaches, execs) is bounded, and a user other than root gets a share of each, so no user can keep the others or root out.

Clients that only look at /run/docker.sock find it with a drop-in, on a host where nothing else has that path:

It answers in the shapes of API 1.51, and of the versions down to 1.24 that clients ask for.

GitLab Runner’s docker executor runs its jobs on nspawn’s machines through the API. Its host setting points at the socket:

A variable’s value can now hold line breaks (-e, compose’s environment, the API’s Env). GitLab’s CI_COMMIT_MESSAGE for a commit with a body is one.

A machine’s API socket takes changes. In 2.0.0 the socket inside a machine was read-only. Now a machine that mounts /var/run/docker.sock, /run/docker.sock or /run/nspawn/api.sock read-write can create, start, exec in and remove containers, pull and remove images, and create volumes and networks. With :ro the socket reads, follows logs and kills, and refuses everything else with 403. Only root inside the machine can connect, and it sees every machine and their -e variables (--secret values never show). A proxy or a dashboard that only reads should mount it :ro, the Traefik example in the 2.0 post included: /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro.

The requirements are the same as for 2.0.0. Packages for Fedora, Debian/Ubuntu and Arch are attached to the release, and apt.nspawn.org and rpm.nspawn.org have the first two. If a client of the Docker API fails against nspawn where it works with docker, open an issue with what it sent.

Where we left it If you used nspawn before, you probably remember it as a small Bash script. nspawn -i //tar read https://hub.nspawn.org/storage/list.txt, picked...

#9878. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.
