#9860. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

#9859. [$] User namespaces + file capabilities = trouble

User namespaces are a key part of the kernel's toolkit for assembling containers; processes within a user namespace can appear to have full root access to the system while gaining no extra privileges in the wider system. At least, that is the intent. In practice, keeping privilege contained within a user namespace has often turned out to be difficult. As an example, consider this small patch series from Josef Bacik, which is intended to address some situations where a process within a user namespace can elevate the privileges of processes outside of it.

#9858. As Russia's Cyberwar Evolves, Belarus Steps Forward

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The "FrostyNeighbor" advanced persistent threat (APT) launched a destructive attack in Ukraine and is raising concerns about deeper alignment with Russian cyber objectives.

Researchers have spotted the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor against a critical target in Ukraine, suggesting Belarus may be upping its support for Russian national objectives — carrying implications for much of Europe.

ESET this week published its APT Activity Report for Q2 and Q3 2026. The report highlights a range of state-sponsored activity across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, but one of the most significant assertions involves Belarus, an Eastern European country that has been close allies with Russia in the latter's invasion of Ukraine.

Historically, Belarusian cyber operations have been tracked separately from those attributed directly to Russian intelligence services, though researchers have long observed overlap in targeting and strategic interests. The Belarusan state-affiliated group FrostyNeighbor — also tracked as UNC1151 — has been known for disinformation and cyber espionage, the latter conducted through various means such as spear phishing and malware.

Related:Russia's Hybrid Cyber-Physical War in Europe Heats Up

While the Eastern European country has also set its sights on Ukrainian and Polish targets in phishing attacks to further its own and possibly Russia's goals, ESET identified a recent escalation in these activities. Mainly, ESET's report notes that its researchers "identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater."

Specifically, FrostyNeighbor deployed Chisel, UltraVNC, Cobalt Strike, and a VBScript wiper via Group Policy against a manufacturing company in Ukraine that ESET said "plays an important role in the country's transportation sector," which is notable because destructive operations up until this point have been explicitly Russia-aligned.

"While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia," the report read. "We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas."

Damien Schaeffer, senior malware researcher at ESET, says that the strongest evidence for an increasing operational closeness with Russia is the number of attacks and the victimology that appears closer to and aligned with Russia's strategic priorities than Belarus's own, as well as a sophistication behind these attacks, "which seems relatively high to Belarus's potential interests alone." He says ESET first observed this trend of increasing aggressiveness at the beginning of 2024.

This comes as North Korea expands its own military cooperation with Russia in the latter's war on Ukraine, which ESET added could mean cyber activity will continue to align as well.

Russia's war on Ukraine stretches far beyond Ukraine, especially in the realm of cyber operations. Russia has grown bolder in cyberattacks particularly against European countries that support Ukraine militarily or politically, are on NATO's eastern flank, and support critical logistics hubs for aid flowing into Ukraine.

This, to varying degrees, has included Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Sweden, Czech Republic, and Germany, among others. In other words, if Russian allies are growing bolder in their cyberactivities explicitly supporting Russia, that carries consequences for all of Europe.

Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, tells Dark Reading that its evidence shows FrostyNeighbor as an actor executing sustained operations and evolving its techniques, though not necessarily an overall increase in operational scale nor shared operational command.

Recorded Future's recommendation is to explicitly track Belarus-linked clusters and correlate their infrastructure, tools, and targeting with Russian threat campaigns "while preserving attribution distinctions."

"Threat models should cover credential theft, persistent access, and the use of compromised accounts to reach additional people. Intelligence collection should include malicious login infrastructure, email exploitation, personal-account targeting, and abuse of trusted contacts, which are the access routes documented in these campaigns," Leslie says. "Defenders do not need proof of Russian tasking to prioritize an actor already targeting them."

While researchers differ on whether Belarusian activity represents deeper operational integration with Russia, they appear to agree that defenders should not dismiss Belarus-linked actors as secondary threats. As Leslie explains, CERT Polska in June 2026 identified UNC1151 as one of the most active APT groups it monitors, "observing new phishing domains almost daily in the preceding weeks."

Organizations in sectors tied to government, transportation, and defense that show support for Ukraine may increasingly encounter campaigns whose objectives align closely with Moscow's broader strategic interests.

He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9857. Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

A security firm patched a decade-old app to prevent the takeover of millions of machines, highlighting that abandoned domains remain a boon to attackers.

When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9855. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗

Rank text‑to‑speech voices via blind A/B listening

Browse speech‑to‑text model performance across datasets

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS."

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard

#9854. Virtualized Redox: from Virtio-FS to Cloud Hypervisor, and beyond

I’m MJ Pooladkhay, and for the past couple of months I have been building a Virtio-FS driver for Redox OS and, more recently, getting Redox to run on Cloud Hypervisor. The driver is merged into the base repository, where most Redox drivers and system components live. The kernel, bootloader and driver changes that let Redox boot to a shell on Cloud Hypervisor are merged too (details below).

Both are fun pieces of work on their own, but they are really the first steps of a bigger effort with two directions:

The guest work is generously funded by NGI Zero Commons and NLnet as part of the Virtualized Redox grant.

Most Internet-facing software today runs in virtual machines, either in the cloud or on edge servers close to its users. Web servers, databases, API backends and microservices spend all day handling input from strangers, and that is where a memory-safe microkernel-based operating system has the most to offer:

This is the direction the project set in its development priorities: Redox as a secure host for web services, first as a private or edge server, and eventually as a multi-tenant cloud server where each tenant is isolated from others.

The easiest way I know to think about a hypervisor is as an operating system whose processes are operating systems. A process runs directly on the CPU until it needs the kernel, for a system call, a page fault or a timer tick, and then the kernel takes over for a moment. A guest OS runs directly on the CPU in the same way, until it does something that only the hypervisor is allowed to handle. That moment a “VM exit” happens where the control is transferred to the hypervisor (similar to how a system call transfers control to the OS kernel). On Linux, KVM in the host kernel handles it, either by itself or by passing it to the virtual machine monitor (VMM), an ordinary process such as Cloud Hypervisor or QEMU. I went through the theory behind this, and why x86 needed new hardware (VT-x and AMD-V) to make it work, in an earlier post on my personal blog.

From Redox’s side, a VM boots much like a laptop does. The virtual CPU starts in firmware, the firmware loads the bootloader from a disk, and the bootloader hands over to the kernel. It’s the same code that runs on real hardware, running natively, with the kernel in supervisor mode (ring 0 on x86) as usual.

Most of what Redox does never leaves the guest. System calls, context switches and page faults are handled by the Redox kernel itself, and the hypervisor doesn’t even see them.

Memory takes a few more steps than on bare metal, because there are now two kernels that each think they own it. Redox’s page tables turn a guest virtual address (GVA) into a guest physical address (GPA), the address Redox believes is in RAM. But guest RAM is really just a big chunk of memory the VMM allocated in its own address space, and the VMM tells KVM which part of it backs which range of guest RAM (a memslot). So every GPA is also a host virtual address (HVA) in the Cloud Hypervisor process, and the host kernel’s page tables turn that into a host physical address (HPA), the actual spot in RAM:

Going through all of that on every memory access would be painfully slow, so KVM collapses the GPA to HPA part into a single step. It builds nested page tables that map guest physical addresses straight to host physical ones, and fills them in lazily as the guest touches memory. The CPU then walks Redox’s page tables and the nested ones together in hardware, and caches the result in the TLB. Redox manages its own page tables freely, and only touching guest memory that isn’t mapped yet causes an exit.

The HVA step has a nice side effect: since guest RAM is an ordinary mapping in the VMM, it can be shared with other host processes. That’s how virtiofsd reads Virtio-FS requests straight out of the guest’s memory, and why sharing a directory requires the guest’s memory to be shared.

Devices are where the hypervisor earns its keep, because every device the guest sees is made up. Some are emulations of real hardware, such as an 8259 interrupt controller, a programmable interval timer (PIT), a serial port or each CPU’s local APIC, and every register access to them is a VM exit that the hypervisor turns into behavior. Others are VirtIO devices, which don’t pretend to be hardware at all and talk to the host through queues in shared memory. Interrupts are made up too. The host keeps the real ones, and the guest only gets the ones the hypervisor injects on behalf of its virtual devices and timers. If the hypervisor doesn’t emulate a device, nobody raises its interrupt (keep that in mind for the ping story below).

In short, the CPU, its timestamp counter (TSC) and the memory are real, and everything else is virtual. The interesting question is which virtual devices you get, and that’s where cloud hypervisors and QEMU part ways.

So far, Redox has been run either on QEMU or on physical hardware. On both, it has leaned on devices that date back to the original IBM PC/AT: a pair of 8259 interrupt controllers, the PIT, a PS/2 keyboard controller, and so on. These are legacy even on real hardware. Modern machines, and OSes such as Linux, route interrupts through the I/O APIC and keep time with each CPU’s local APIC timer. Redox kept using the old devices mainly because it didn’t support the ACPI pieces needed to set up their replacements.

Hypervisors built for the cloud, such as Cloud Hypervisor and Firecracker, drop most of the legacy devices. Cloud Hypervisor gives a guest its CPUs (each with a local APIC), memory, an I/O APIC, a serial port, a real-time clock (RTC), a minimal ACPI platform and a handful of VirtIO devices. Not much else. Fewer emulated devices means less code in the hypervisor for a guest to poke at, and less for the guest OS to probe and set up at boot.

These hypervisors can also skip firmware entirely and jump straight into the kernel (PVH direct boot). Redox doesn’t do that yet and still boots through UEFI firmware.

I would say Redox is a very good fit for minimal VMs like these. A VM that runs a single service doesn’t need a USB stack, a sound daemon or a desktop, and since those are all ordinary userspace daemons on Redox, leaving them out is a matter of not putting them in the image.

What goes into the image, and what runs once it boots, is a short TOML file in the build system. Init services are small TOML files too, so an image can just as well boot straight into a web server, with no one logging in.

The server demo config is an example of this, with SSH, PHP and the nginx configuration.

Virtio-FS lets a VM use a directory that lives on the host. The virtio-fsd Redox daemon talks to the virtiofsd Linux daemon on the host using the FUSE protocol, carried over virtqueues. Each shared directory appears as its own scheme, /scheme/virtio-fs., named after the tag the host gives it, so a share can be put in or left out of a process’s namespace like any other scheme. You can share more than one directory at a time.

Under the hood, the driver keeps its own cache of inodes and directory entries, and tells the host to forget the ones it hasn’t used in a while (FUSE_FORGET, driven by an LRU cache). The driver works on both QEMU and Cloud Hypervisor, and comes with a test suite.

Getting Redox to a working shell on Cloud Hypervisor was mostly a matter of finding every place where it assumed it was running natively on a PC, as well as a few other gotchas:

QEMU’s q35 machine does have an 8259 interrupt controller and an HPET, so Redox keeps using them there exactly as before.

My favorite bug was this one: with networking up, ping -c 4 1.1.1.1 got a reply in about 15 ms and then… just sat there, until I interrupted it:

So the NIC, the route and the NAT on the host were all fine. Then where did the other three packets go?

They were never sent! ping sends the first echo right away, then asks the time scheme to wake it up one second later. In the kernel, that wakeup is posted by timeout::trigger, and the only caller of timeout::trigger was the PIT interrupt handler (on QEMU, the HPET drives the same interrupt line). Cloud Hypervisor has neither a PIT nor an HPET, so that handler never ran.

Reading the clock still worked, since kvmclock converts the CPU’s TSC to nanoseconds whenever someone asks, which is why the first reply had a sensible round-trip time. But nothing was ticking. Every ping -i, and every other wait on the time scheme, was waiting for an interrupt that was never going to come, and a nanosleep only woke up when something else happened to run the scheduler. The same handler also drives the scheduler’s preemption tick, so the system had quietly become cooperative: a process only gave up the CPU when it blocked or yielded.

The fix is to use a timer every x86 CPU already has: its local APIC timer. When there is no HPET, each CPU now arms its own local APIC timer in TSC-deadline mode, where you tell it the TSC value at which the next interrupt should fire. The tick period is converted from nanoseconds to TSC ticks using the same scale kvmclock already provides1. The handler then does the PIT handler’s old job, posting expired timeouts and driving the scheduler tick. With that in place, ping -c 4 sends all four packets, one second apart, and Redox is preemptive again!

Booting to a shell is a good start, but it’s not yet something you would deploy. Here’s a look at the remaining work, which is also covered by the current NLnet grant:

Once the list above is done, Redox should work like any other cloud image: you launch it, it picks up its hostname and SSH key on first boot, and you log in and run your services.

The same pieces also fit more specific uses, such as short-lived instances for CI and testing, and sandboxes for AI agents (more on that one below).

Whatever runs inside the VM, Redox can stack three layers of isolation around it:

To reach the host, a misbehaving tool would have to break through all three.

A minimal image and Virtio-FS fit together nicely, because they split a system into the part that never changes and the part that has to survive.

The image holds the kernel, the drivers and the service, and nothing writes to it. Every instance boots from exactly the same bytes, an upgrade becomes just booting a new image, and a rollback is booting the old one. Redox can already run a live image entirely from memory, and the system could eventually live in InitFS, the in-memory filesystem Redox boots from, with no RedoxFS image at all.

Everything that has to outlive the VM, such as databases, uploads and logs, lives on the host and reaches the guest through Virtio-FS. Each share is just a scheme, so the service only gets the shares it needs, and its configuration can come in as a read-only share. Throw the VM away, boot a new image, point it at the same shares, and the data is still there.

The only catch is that Virtio-FS needs the virtiofsd daemon running on the host, next to the hypervisor. It’s the same mechanism Kata Containers uses to give its VMs their files. On machines you run yourself (a server, an edge box, a bare-metal cloud instance, or a cloud VM with nested virtualization), setting it up is easy. Regular public cloud VMs and Firecracker don’t offer Virtio-FS, so there the persistent part goes on an ordinary attached disk instead, which already works (Redox boots on Google Cloud, for example).

One potentially interesting use case is sandboxing AI agents, which needs every one of these pieces. Agents run code and tools that nobody has reviewed, and the usual answer is a throwaway VM for each task. On Redox, that VM starts from a small image or a snapshot. The agent’s tool runner gets its working folder and only the other schemes it actually needs, and tools compiled to WebAssembly add another layer on top. The agent’s workspace is a Virtio-FS share, so its changes land on the host as soon as it makes them, and the orchestrator talks to it over virtio-vsock. When the task is done, the VM is thrown away.

The second direction flips the picture. As a guest, Redox runs on top of Linux, and Linux’s drivers deal with the real hardware.

As a host, it would be the other way around. Redox runs on the hardware and uses its own drivers for the devices it supports, and a small Linux guest takes care of the ones it doesn’t (say, a network card with no Redox driver yet). The device is handed to the guest through PCI passthrough (VFIO on the Linux side), and Linux offers it back to Redox through VirtIO. Instead of all of Linux’s drivers or none of them, Redox gets to choose, and each borrowed driver can be replaced by a native one when it’s ready. This is the “hosted Linux for driver support” idea from the development priorities, and FreeBSD already does something similar with bhyve and wifibox, where a small Linux VM drives the Wi-Fi card.

Redox has explored hosting VMs before, with Revirt during RSoC 2022, and now we have a solid plan for it:

The kernel would gain AMD SVM support, exposed through a new kernel scheme. It would own only what a guest must never be able to change: SVM enablement, the VMCB (the structure that holds a guest’s state and decides what causes an exit), the nested page tables, the virtual local APIC and the switch between host and guest. Everything else would live in an ordinary Redox process, the VMM, which creates the VM, supplies its devices and handles its exits. It’s the same split as KVM and QEMU on Linux, but done the Redox way, through a scheme instead of ioctls.

The VMM would be a small program built on the rust-vmm crates (vm-memory, virtio-queue and linux-loader), not a port of Cloud Hypervisor or QEMU, and it wouldn’t clone /dev/kvm either. Its register and exit records would be KVM-compatible, though, so a Cloud Hypervisor or QEMU backend stays possible later.

Intel VT-x guests are future work, but VT-d will be implemented.

And what would tie both directions together? A Redox guest booting on a Redox host.

See how to run Redox on Cloud Hypervisor.

To share a directory from your host with a Redox VM over Virtio-FS, follow this guide.

If you want to help, or just follow along, join us on Matrix and take a look at the global issue tracker.

The period is computed once, from the kvmclock scale at boot. If the VM is migrated to a host with a different TSC frequency, the tick rate changes with it. That one is on my TODO list. ↩︎

#9853. L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

I ricercatori non riescono a spiegare del tutto perché le minacce informatiche in Italia siano così diverse rispetto a quelle di qualsiasi altro Paese.

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

Secondo nuovi dati, l’Italia è vittima di un numero sproporzionatamente elevato di attacchi informatici. Non solo: le tipologie di attacchi che colpiscono le organizzazioni nel Paese sono molto diverse da quelle che colpiscono altre località. I ricercatori avanzano tre teorie per spiegarne il motivo.

È vero che alcune regioni e alcuni paesi sono esposti a un rischio informatico maggiore a causa di fattori economici, militari e politici. Israele è una calamita per gli hacktivisti e per le minacce persistenti avanzate (APT) regionali, legate agli Stati. La storia unica del Brasile lo rende un vero e proprio alveare di trojan bancari. L’economia degli Stati Uniti attirerà sempre la massima attenzione da parte dei truffatori. Non è però così ovvio il motivo per cui l’Italia sia un bersaglio così popolare per i criminali informatici.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

«Uno dei motivi principali per cui abbiamo deciso di esaminare il panorama delle minacce in Italia è che il Paese continuava a comparire in cima alle nostre statistiche nei rapporti interni mensili», afferma Gianluca Tiepolo, analista di criminalità informatica presso Intel471. In un rapporto condiviso in esclusiva con Dark Reading prima della sua pubblicazione, Intel471 ha rilevato che l’Italia rappresenta un vero e proprio caso a sé stante nel panorama globale delle minacce informatiche. Le organizzazioni italiane subiscono attacchi a un ritmo ben superiore a quanto ci si potrebbe ragionevolmente aspettare, considerando le dimensioni del Paese, la sua economia e la sua situazione politica. Inoltre, gli attacchi sfruttanti le vulnerabilità e le infrastrutture web sono molto più comuni in Italia che altrove.

«Volevamo capire cosa fosse alla base di quelle statistiche», afferma Tiepolo. Alla fine, però, i dati dipingono un quadro quasi inspiegabile di ciò che sta accadendo nella terra della pasta e del Chianti.

L’Italia è il 25° Paese più grande al mondo ma, secondo questi nuovi dati, le sue organizzazioni rappresentano circa il 7% di tutti i dati di accesso iniziale venduti sui forum dei criminali informatici. A livello globale, è seconda solo agli Stati Uniti (30%). L’Italia si colloca inoltre al quarto posto tra i Paesi più presi di mira dal ransomware.

Ancora più strani sono i tipi di intrusioni informatiche che colpiscono le organizzazioni in Italia. Secondo i nuovi dati, gli initial access broker (IAB) hanno ottenuto il loro primo punto d’appoggio sfruttando vulnerabilità nel 57% dei casi. Le credenziali hanno spiegato solo il 23% dei casi. Nel frattempo, gli IAB hanno venduto l’accesso all’infrastruttura web di proprietà delle vittime nel 49% dei casi, con strumenti di accesso remoto e desktop remoto che rappresentano il 26% dei casi.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

E allora? Forse queste cifre non saltano all’occhio. Ora, però, confrontiamole con i dati di Intel471 tratti dal suo rapporto “2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook”:

A livello globale nel 2025, gli IAB hanno preso di mira gli strumenti di accesso remoto e di desktop remoto nel 67% dei casi — il 41% in più, in termini relativi, rispetto all’Italia. Nel frattempo, l’infrastruttura web — di gran lunga la risorsa più a rischio in Italia — rappresentava una frazione talmente esigua dei dati globali di Intel471 che l’azienda non si è nemmeno preoccupata di citarla nel proprio rapporto.

Allo stesso modo, secondo i dati globali dell’azienda, gli attacchi basati sulle credenziali sono oggi, in generale, otto volte più comuni di qualsiasi altro tipo di attacco. È emerso che il 49% delle inserzioni su IAB indicava le credenziali come tipo di attacco, rispetto al 23% dei dati specifici per l’Italia. E, cosa davvero esilarante, mentre in Italia rappresentano circa il 57% di tutti gli attacchi, le vulnerabilità sfruttate sono emerse solo nel 6,5% dei casi a livello globale.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Sebbene i dati sulla sicurezza informatica possano essere interpretati in modi diversi a seconda delle circostanze, l’Italia sembra davvero una sorta di “unicorno” del rischio informatico, afferma Tiepolo, aggiungendo che l’Italia è ormai da tempo in ritardo in termini di preparazione informatica.

«Sono italiano», dice. «Ho lavorato con molti clienti italiani diversi. Quello che posso dire è che l’Italia è probabilmente leggermente indietro rispetto ad altri paesi europei, semplicemente in termini di [adozione delle] tecnologie di sicurezza. Ad esempio, le tecnologie di rilevamento e risposta sugli endpoint (EDR) sono diventate popolari in Italia intorno al 2020–2021. Prima del 2020, la maggior parte delle aziende italiane non utilizzava la tecnologia EDR. Quindi, forse storicamente, l’Italia è un po’ indietro nell’investire effettivamente in prodotti e tecnologie di sicurezza informatica».

Inoltre, i criminali informatici opportunisti stanno sfruttando in massa vulnerabilità note, diffuse e spesso piuttosto datate per mietere un numero maggiore di vittime in Italia rispetto ad altri paesi. «I dati che abbiamo visto la scorsa settimana da PHP2Shell, credo, confermano questa valutazione. L’Italia è il paese europeo con il maggior numero di versioni PHP 4, 5 e 7, che sono ormai fuori supporto», osserva Tiepolo.

«Ben il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale rivolte all’Italia sono quelle che chiamiamo “offerte all’ingrosso”», ipotizza. «Non si tratta di offerte mirate specificatamente all’Italia, ma semplicemente di sfruttamento delle vulnerabilità. La nostra valutazione è che l’Italia sia probabilmente più lenta di altri paesi nell’applicare le patch ai propri sistemi».

Un’altra possibilità correlata è che l’Italia si trovi vittima di una sorta di effetto rete delle vulnerabilità informatiche. La logica è più o meno questa: se determinate tecnologie sono particolarmente diffuse in un paese come l’Italia e le organizzazioni sono lente nell’affrontare le vulnerabilità di tali tecnologie, allora quel paese diventa un’economia di scala attraente.

Come ha scritto Intel471 nel proprio rapporto: «Una volta che un attore sviluppa un metodo di sfruttamento efficace, può applicare tale metodo ad altri sistemi esposti senza dover condurre un’attività di ricognizione separata ed estesa contro ciascuna organizzazione. Ciò riduce lo sforzo necessario per compromettere aziende la cui dimensione o il cui profilo potrebbero altrimenti offrire un incentivo limitato per un’intrusione mirata».

I ricercatori non hanno potuto specificare esattamente a quali tecnologie, vulnerabilità o metodi di sfruttamento questa teoria possa riferirsi, ma hanno osservato che essa si inserisce nel dato secondo cui il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale alle organizzazioni italiane online viene venduto all’ingrosso.

Senza avallare specificatamente i dati o le conclusioni di Intel471, i rappresentanti della società di sicurezza informatica Cleafy, con sede a Milano, hanno dichiarato a Dark Reading di aver osservato modelli sostanzialmente simili.

«La nostra ricerca sulle minacce evidenzia effettivamente un modello correlato: gli autori degli attacchi riutilizzano strumenti, infrastrutture e tecniche per estendere le campagne a diversi obiettivi bancari italiani», ha scritto l’azienda via e-mail. Ha citato casi come il kit di iniezione web drIBAN, che gli autori degli attacchi hanno utilizzato per sfruttare il sistema di Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC), ampiamente diffuso in Italia. Casi come quello di drIBAN «non dimostrano che l’Italia abbia un mercato di accesso iniziale sproporzionatamente ampio, ma illustrano come le tecniche di attacco e le infrastrutture riutilizzabili possano aiutare i criminali informatici a estendere le operazioni su più obiettivi».

C’è un altro fattore, potenzialmente significativo, che spiega perché l’Italia appaia così diversa dagli altri paesi nei set di dati sugli attacchi informatici: la prevalenza delle piccole imprese.

La maggior parte delle imprese, ovunque, è di piccole dimensioni, ma, almeno rispetto ad altre economie avanzate, ciò è particolarmente vero in Italia. Una “panoramica dei dati per l’Italia” del maggio 2024 redatta da McKinsey ha rilevato che le “MSME” — micro, piccole e medie imprese — hanno contribuito all’economia e all’occupazione italiane in misura superiore di circa il 10% rispetto alla loro quota relativa in altre economie avanzate. Lo scorso marzo, inoltre, l’Organizzazione per la cooperazione e lo sviluppo economico (OCSE) ha pubblicato un rapporto in cui si indicava che nel 2023 il 99,9% delle imprese italiane era costituito da PMI e il 94,8% da microimprese.

«L’Italia ha molte piccole e medie imprese», afferma Tiepolo. «Una delle cose emerse dai dati — in particolare quelli relativi alle estorsioni — è che questi gruppi prendono di mira [in modo sproporzionato] le piccole e medie imprese. Quindi questo potrebbe essere uno dei motivi per cui [l’Italia si distingue] rispetto ad altri paesi che hanno un maggior numero di grandi aziende».

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9852. AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into new executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

For example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We plan to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

InfoQ Homepage News TypeScript 7.1 Beta: Restores the Compiler API and Makes Vue and Svelte First-Class

Nov 06, 2026 3 min read

Microsoft has released TypeScript 7.1 Beta, the first update to the Go-based native compiler that landed as TypeScript 7.0 in July, and the release that finally hands tool authors a programmatic API again. Daniel Rosenwasser announced the beta on 20 October 2026, and the team pointed developers to it on X, inviting feedback ahead of a release candidate and stable build that the iteration plan tentatively places in late November, though the beta itself arrived two weeks behind schedule.

The headline change restores the compiler API that 7.0 dropped. For three months anything that embedded the compiler, from Vue’s Volar to Svelte, Astro, ts-morph and type-aware linting, was stranded on TypeScript 6. Rather than revive the old monolithic module, 7.1 splits it into focused entry points such as typescript/sync, typescript/async, typescript/fs and typescript/ast, paths that previously sat behind an unstable prefix now dropped to signal intent. The client also models incremental edits through reusable snapshots, so an editor can derive new state from an old one without rebuilding the world, and the team says the surface will stay backward compatible across all of 7.x once stable.

Sitting on top of that is the beta’s most discussed feature, content mappers, a supported plugin point that lets a package hand TypeScript a virtual view of a non-standard file such as a .vue or .svelte component, with mappings back to the original so errors point at the right line. Because a mapper runs as a separate process it executes only when you opt in, and the team warns the flag should be treated like any build plugin.

Vue’s language tools are already porting to it: maintainer Johnson Chu has shipped Vue Language Tools v4 alpha on top of content mappers, dropping the separate vue-tsc binary in favour of a @vue/content-mapper that runs inside tsc itself. In a hands-on migration write-up, the Directus admin app, 581 Vue components across 882 TypeScript files saw type checks fall from 14.19 to 3.10 seconds on tsc 7.1 plus the mapper, a 4.6x speedup over vue-tsc 3. The author also flagged that teams adopting the beta would need to run 7.1 in CI alongside an older TypeScript in the editor until Vue tooling stabilises on top of the stable release.

Microsoft’s MUI docs benchmark falls from 22.2 to 11.9 seconds while roughly halving memory, though heavier codebases such as VS Code see closer to 1.2x. An independent test against NestJS put a 353,000 line check at 2.76 seconds on the beta against 4.95 on 7.0 and 12.42 on the old compiler, while flagging a 7.0 memory regression that 7.1 reverses.

On GitHub, Akira Higuchi reported that, in a particular editor workflow, saving a mapper’s watched configuration file could leave types stale until the language server is restarted. The issue remains open.

The language itself gains import attributes in ambient module declarations, TC39 source phase imports for loading WebAssembly, and a stable es2026 target carrying additions like Math.sumPrecise() and Error.isError().

Teams still on TypeScript 5 should move through 6 to 7, and projects using Vue, Svelte or Angular should keep a dual TypeScript 6 and 7 install until their framework tooling ships a 7.1 build. Tool and library authors are urged to port to the new entry points now and to flag missing functions through the API status tracker while gaps can still be filled before stable. The independent numbers are a reminder that the native compiler now sets the bar, with rival type checkers on Hacker News already measuring themselves against tsgo 7.1 beta.

TypeScript is an open-source programming language developed and maintained by Microsoft. It builds on JavaScript by adding optional static typing, catching errors before code runs and making large codebases easier to build and maintain with confidence. Since version 7.0 its compiler has been written in Go rather than in TypeScript itself, a native port that underpins the speed gains in this release, and it remains widely adopted across the frontend and backend ecosystems, with first-class support in frameworks such as React, Angular, Vue and Node.js.
