#9849. Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

A recent law enforcement operation to dismantle harmful scam centers was a big success. A threat intelligence expert walks us through what happened and why he wants more of the same.

Pushes for public-private partnerships to address escalating cyber threats have been on the industry's radar for years. Collaboration has been a focal point in cybersecurity conference panels and government initiatives. Calls for more information-sharing and analysis centers have been persistent.

As director of preemptive cyberdefense at Silent Push, Michael Sweeney had a front-row seat to this kind of partnership when his company recently took part in "Operation Blackout," a coordinated international operation to take down criminal networks operating out of West Africa.

Operation Blackout coordinated efforts by the UK's National Crime Agency, the US Department of Justice (DoJ), the FBI, and private industry partners — including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Silent Push — to disrupt criminal networks behind pig-butchering, romance, and cryptocurrency scams. The DoJ announced that the campaign resulted in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and the removal of more than 3.7 million fake social media accounts.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

As the UK's main law enforcement agency, the National Crime Agency hosted Joint Disruption Week in London in early October to bring together the DoJ and the FBI with private industry partners to share real-time intelligence. In addition to US authorities and private industry partners, the Nigerian Joint Case Team on Cybercrimes, the Nigeria Police Force-National Cybercrime Center, and Ghanaian Cyber Security Authority also participated.

The Joint Disruption Week marked the first coordinated effort specifically focused on West Africa, according to the DoJ, which noted that global commitments are essential to dismantling the far-reaching scam centers.

The goal of these operations is to tackle scam activity at the global scale it has reached today, Sweeney explains. The more people who participate, the "better off we are," he says.

"The idea is not only to stop the current scams, but also to look across all of these different events," Sweeney tells Dark Reading. "[Industry and government are] all needed together in order to get this successfully taken down."

Data taken from scams reported through the FBI's Internet Complaint Center and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre formed the initial basis for Operation Blackout. From there, law enforcement compiled information, including the domains the scammers used and the infrastructure they set up to manipulate people for money.

Then the collaboration really began. Meta provided some of the data that helped drill down to specific regions — a surprising move, since social media platforms don't generally cooperate with law enforcement, despite threat actors abusing platforms to lure in victims. Several other organizations sent signals to further paint a picture of the attacker's intent and infrastructure.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

Silent Push's role involved providing 35,000 domains, creating more than 70 detection rules to trigger alerts when malicious activity occurs, and fingerprinting, Sweeney says. All of those are considered the "common choke points" that help researchers and authorities map the threat actors' network patterns.

Everything was analyzed, and the data augmented each other to provide the evidence authorities needed to take down the scammers, Sweeney says.

"Once you get everyone in the room with all the data, it becomes easier to see the big picture," he says. "From that, see where the attacks are coming from, the commonalities, and who is the most important person to take down in the operation, and where you want to go to get these people."

Sweeney attributes the success of Operation Blackout and other operations he has worked on over the years to how clear the mission was; everyone was on the same page about the goals and importance of data sharing, he says. Many of the legal or jurisdiction blockers that would otherwise prevent them from sharing information and hinder actual action were removed, including data-sharing agreements with users.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

A number of providers were also involved, including Starlink. While each platform offers different services, they united in a shared stance. The camaraderie and energy that accompanied it were palpable, Sweeney says.

"We come together [to] say, 'If you're abusing our services, we're going to do everything we can to stop you, and we're going to pull in law enforcement,'" he says.

One thing Sweeney would like to change is the pace; he would like to see these partnerships move faster and conduct more operations as scammers drain billions from the US economy. Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence.

Sweeney says the people who just report a scam or who are too ashamed to come forward at all draw him to this work. They should know they aren't alone and that people are working hard to fight back, he adds.

"Everyone really wants to stop it, so pacing may be the only frustration," Sweeney says. "Let's do more. Hit them while they're down so that more people don't have that moment where they're having to figure out how to report a scam.”

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9848. Devs Hit by Trojanized Claude Code Extension for Cursor

Two serious security issues hit Cursor on the same day, highlighting the risks for AI-powered integrated development environments (IDEs).

Anthropic's official Claude Code extension for the Cursor VS Code Marketplace was hijacked and swapped out for a malicious version with a persistent backdoor.

The SolarWinds-style attack in miniature lasted only 11 hours, from 9:27 a.m. GMT to 8:35 p.m. GMT, on Oct. 29, according to Cursor's disclosure. Any software developers who downloaded or updated Claude Code in their Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) during that time would have received a malicious version 2.1.313, which pilfered sensitive data from infected machines and, in a minority of cases, could have allowed attackers persistent, privileged access to users' systems.

Cursor stated that "at most 5,000 users were affected" and that they will be contacted about the incident directly.

Separately that same day, researchers described an unrelated exploit in Cursor, allowing attackers to deploy arbitrary code to developers' machines via Cursor's built-in browser.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

Cursor did not immediately respond to an inquiry from Dark Reading regarding both of these stories.

For some, the notion of a compromised "extension" might evoke browser extensions, which are so frequently vulnerable, suspicious, and outright malicious that cybersecurity news concerning them tends not to cause much panic, even in extreme cases.

Extensions in coding environments are a different beast. "IDE extensions are scarier than browser extensions because, unlike browser extensions, they are designed to have the same level of permissions as their host," Gal Weizman, security researcher at Forever Security, tells Dark Reading. "They can run code, access the filesystem, fire network requests, and more."

On Oct. 29, an attacker tried to leverage the power afforded by coding environment extensions by sneaking a 66-line loader on top of the real extension's legitimate code. According to an analysis from the community threat intelligence platform OpenSourceMalware, everything about the extension remained the same except for this lone edit to its extension.js file.

As soon as the extension loaded — without need for the user to establish a Claude conversation — the new file is revved up. It attempts to add an attacker-controlled key to victims' SSH configurations, with the goal of establishing reverse tunnels that act as a backdoor into the compromised systems.

The malicious extension also attempts to make those connections persistent by registering background processes — for macOS systems, a LaunchAgent; and for Windows, scheduled tasks running with system privileges, plus a fallback Startup script. This whole business was doomed from the start, Cursor wrote, since turning on the local SSH service requires administrative privileges, which the Claude Code extension only possesses in "highly unusual circumstances."

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Victims weren't totally out of the woods, though, as the malicious code also exfiltrated system information via separate Web requests. Stolen data was limited to hostnames, usernames, operating systems (OSes), OS architectures, home directory paths, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git emails, and public IP addresses.

Cursor's public disclosure suggests that the security incident was its own, not Anthropic's. The malicious version "was not developed by Anthropic," the SpaceX-owned company reported.

In response to the discovery, Cursor took a variety of steps to protect itself: rotating its keys, checking for tampering in other extensions, and taking its marketplace temporarily offline and rebuilding it. It also worked with the relevant cloud hosting provider to take down the attacker's malicious infrastructure.

Cursor did not specify how the intrusion occurred in the first place. While acknowledging that it's not yet known what happened here, Weizman explains, "Historically, the most common way extensions and plug-ins get hijacked is through theft of locally stored credentials that allow publishing new versions of these packages."

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

"Enabling 2FA for publishing such extensions is an excellent way to significantly mitigate such risk in the future. Relying on an access token as the only gate for pushing such critical software significantly increases the risk of this happening," he says.

On the same day of the Anthropic Cursor attack, Weizman published separate research detailing weaknesses in the browsers built into top desktop AI assistants today, which could be exploited to devastating effect. His test cases included Claude Desktop, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Cursor. Cursor has arguably the worst issue of the bunch.

In his experiments, Weizman's team created a clean-looking website, with a visible HTML chip concealing a malicious shell command in its attributes. Then they opened up the site in a built-in Cursor browser. "When the command hit Cursor's safety sandbox and was blocked, the agent — on its own, with nothing in the page telling it to — switched the sandbox off and tried again. The control worked. The agent talked itself out of using it," Weizman wrote in the report.

The attack didn't work universally across all models. When it did work, the browser escape allowed the researchers to deploy an arbitrary app to their test victim's computer. And just like the malicious Claude Code extension, the app ran with the victim's full permissions. Cursor did not respond to Forever Security's disclosure, but the company quietly patched the issue on Oct. 1.

“IDEs are becoming more agentic. They're being given agentic capabilities, which can introduce dangerous architecture. It can be very risky when things go wrong," Weizman says.

"Here we've had two examples of that: built-in browsers, and what happened with Claude Code, both of which impacted Cursor," he concludes. "And because of the rapid pace at which this is happening, security isn't necessarily keeping up."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9847. The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1)

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:

#9846. Seven stable kernels with fixes for three Xen vulnerabilities

Hot on the heels of the previous two stable kernels, Greg Kroah-Hartman has announced the release of the 7.3.3, 6.18.62, 6.12.116, 6.6.162, 6.1.192, 5.15.225, and 5.10.274 stable kernels. Each one only contains fixes for three use-after-free vulnerabilities announced today by the Xen security team.

Two of the vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial of service (DoS) for the entire Xen host machine with possible information leakage (CVE-2026-100080, CVE-2026-100082), and one may allow privilege escalation as well as a DoS of the host machine (CVE-2026-100081). Users should, of course, upgrade if they are using Xen.

#9845. What can I realistically do with local AI on a Mac mini M5 Pro (48GB)?

I just got a Mac mini with an M5 Pro (base CPU config) and 48GB of unified memory. I want to run as much AI locally as makes sense, but it's hard to separate what actually works day to day from benchmark hype.

Real tokens/sec numbers and "this was a waste of time" stories are especially welcome.

Qwen3.8-27B is by far the best coding model runnable locally. However, it will be difficult to hold a long context window, and forget about running multiple coding sessions in parallel. It's also going to be annoyingly slow for interactive work. It can be useful if you give it chores to do in the background or overnight. It can be useful as a secondary model like advisor role in oh-my-pi.

Unfortunately, other models smaller than 27B are too dumb for coding (in serious projects you'll get more bugs than help from them).

4-bit quants are optimal for small RAM budget. Going lower starts breaking the models and higher quants give you diminishing results.

gemma4-e4b is small and pretty fast, and works fine as a lossy wikipedia and a smarter regex (searching and summarization where accuracy isn't critical), but don't let it edit anything that you want to keep.

Comfy stuff tends to fit easily in 48GB, but it's a bit slow (most workflows are designed for nvidia cards with less VRAM and more raw power).

I've got 48GB M3 Max and 96GB M5 Ultra. The 96GB is still barely usable for real coding, and financially doesn't make sense compared to Deepseek 4.1 Flash that's smarter, 4x faster than anything I can run, and doesn't OOM when I run more than a couple things at once.

However, it will be difficult to hold a long context window

This might improve a bit if a Qwen4 27b is released since Qwen4 will be replacing the dense attention layers with sparse attention layers.

EDIT: Actually no, I forgot QSA still keeps the full kv cache representation around and only compresses for selection purposes, unlike DSV4.1 which uses the compressed version for attention as well. So performance is improved but not memory usage.

I have the same hardware as you and I've been using MLX-LM with Qwen3.6-35B 6bit quant. My setup is a vibe-coded local server that just wires together a bunch of different components with a web UI. It's fairly fast in terms of token output, but noticeably worse than claude at coding. It can handle routine tasks and I've been using it to scan my codebase for bugs. Low-powered models work pretty well for finding bugs if you make them verify the bug is real. I was also using it for some voice assistant stuff (with a separate speech-to-text and text-to-speech setup) and it was pretty good at handling natural language questions and using tools accordingly (turn the lights on, play music, etc.). I got it to a point where the latency was extremely low and it felt really responsive. As for image generation, the version I was able to get running on my home setup was drastically worse than the big company offerings and I didn't really have much use for it, so I abandoned that part.

That I pay my own power bill is satisfying for part but not all of the ethics problem. I look forward to a local setup being good enough for most anybody, so we can in some form give back to the commons what we took.

For now I'm constrained by models being either too slow on this chip to wait for, or too dumb to depend on. I don't just mean they write bugs, I mean sometimes they think their way into a non-converging fugue state I must abort. But they are much smarter per time than two years ago when I first explored this, and the DIY aspect is fun.

For general questions, I'm happy enough with Siri AI. It's fine for a first try and that's often plenty. And local + PCC is usually private enough.

For automated coding tasks whose results I'll depend on to be good, I'd go back to the two major players and get a subscription again. I don't have one today, but I'd get whichever is not on tap at work.

Check out Unbiased Strata which aims to be a more secure version of Strata. It's a custom inference engine based on llama.cpp (?) tuned to let you run Qwen-Flash-Next locally using as little as 12GB VRAM (plus 96GB RAM). It works by predicting which MoE parameters will activate and hot-loading them into VRAM before they are needed.

I have a 12GB Nvidia GPU on my framework laptop and have been running this for a month or two. It's the best local LLM setup I've used by far. I mostly use it with the Pi harness, which took a little tuning to get the context window and certain token limits right. I don't have hard numbers off the top of my head but I've found it to be a little slower than Opus, and still very usable. You can probably get higher speeds on 48GB.

InfoQ Homepage News GitLab 19.5 Makes Agentic Development a Governed Part of the DevOps Platform

Nov 06, 2026 3 min read

GitLab 19.5, released on October 15, puts agentic software development and governance at the centre of the platform, making its GitLab MCP server generally available while expanding how external AI agents can interact with GitLab.

The release allows MCP-compatible tools such as Claude Code and Cursor to access GitLab's broader tool catalogue and invoke GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and flows. At the same time, GitLab is adding controls for governing those external agents, giving security teams visibility into which agents are being used, by whom, and against which projects.

The generally available GitLab MCP server provides agents with access to GitLab capabilities through the Model Context Protocol. New tools allow agents to discover groups, inspect individual CI/CD artifact files, and start or monitor GitLab Duo agents and flows. Administrators can also select which MCP toolsets are exposed, reducing unnecessary tools and the context they consume.

Giving an agent every available tool increases both context consumption and the number of actions the model could potentially take. Toolset selection provides a relatively simple form of least-privilege agent design.

GitLab.com also introduces MCP rate limits of 60 requests per minute for Free users and 600 for Premium and Ultimate users, with reconnects and retries counting towards the limit.

One of the more significant additions is the ability to bring Externally Connected Agents into GitLab's AI Governance capabilities.

Previously, the AI Governance Dashboard focused on GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents. GitLab 19.5 allows tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex to be connected through the GitLab CLI. Once configured, organisations can record qualifying agent sessions, including the user, agent, project, and timing, with activity appearing alongside GitLab's own agents. Audit events can also be streamed to a SIEM.

This is an important step beyond simply providing an MCP endpoint. Connectivity creates capability; governance determines whether that capability can be safely used at organisational scale.

GitLab Duo CLI also gains an auto mode, allowing agents to execute tools without requesting approval for every shell command, Git operation, or MCP call. The feature is disabled by default and can be controlled at instance, group, and project levels, while tools explicitly marked Always Deny remain blocked.

The /goal command is also now generally available, allowing developers to describe an open-ended objective and have GitLab Duo delegate implementation and verification to a governed flow.

Together, these features move GitLab closer to an agent operating model in which developers provide intent while agents execute multiple steps across the development environment.

That makes the governance controls increasingly important: the more autonomous the agent becomes, the less practical it is to rely on a human approving every individual action.

The release also makes GitLab Secrets Manager generally available. Built on OpenBao, it integrates with existing GitLab group and project permissions, scopes secrets to the jobs that require them, and generates audit events for secret operations.

GitLab is also expanding security configuration profiles, allowing organisations to centrally customise settings such as excluded paths, analyzer images and full-history scans for Secret Detection and SAST rather than repeating configuration in every project's CI/CD file.

These changes complement the agent features by strengthening the controls around the repositories, credentials, and pipelines that agents may access.

GitLab's direction increasingly resembles GitHub's strategy of turning coding agents into participants in the software lifecycle, but GitLab is placing particular emphasis on connecting external agents to its existing DevSecOps governance model.

GitHub's ecosystem benefits from the reach of GitHub Copilot and coding agents, while tools such as Cursor and Claude Code focus more heavily on the developer's local environment. GitLab's MCP approach instead attempts to make the DevOps platform itself agent-accessible, including repositories, issues, pipelines, artifacts, and GitLab-native agents.

The competitive question GitLab is looking at is moving beyond which coding assistant generates better code to which platform provides the safest and most useful environment for autonomous agents to perform engineering work.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9843. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

#9842. Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The cybersecurity market is difficult to predict, but a glimpse into the annual DataTribe Challenge shows what's trending and what's not.

Startups have been battling it out on the DataTribe Challenge stage for the past nine years, but this year's event still saw some firsts.

A cyber insurance company made the top five finalists, and attendees got to vote for their favorite finalist with the People's Choice Award. Both of these firsts highlighted how people are looking for answers to new risks introduced by artificial intelligence (AI).

The DataTribe Challenge, hosted by the cyber startup foundry and venture capital firm, is one of the signature events of its annual Cyber Innovation Conference. The meeting, which took place in October, aims to unite the cybersecurity ecosystem, from founders to investors and — since it's held in Washington, D.C. — some policymakers, too.

Cybersecurity conferences pop up on the calendar more frequently these days; that momentum is important "to keep the information fresh" as the industry and threat landscape transforms rapidly, explains Robert Ackerman, co-founder and managing partner at DataTribe. Game-changing incidents that require sharing information emerge almost daily now, he adds, pointing to the more recent PHP2Shell vulnerability that attackers jumped on and proved difficult for organizations to patch.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

An expanding pool of cyber-related startups is also driving industry transformation. Nearly 700 rising companies submitted entries or were considered for this year's Challenge, which pairs startups with mentors before they pitch to judges who crown the winner.

As Ackerman and Leo Scott, managing director at DataTribe, filtered down the contestants into the top five list, they found it interesting that many of the startups focused on the dynamics around how AI is driving the market as organizations transition from AI adoption to managing the technology.

Some companies had a more direct tie. This year's winner, Sondera, aims to solve agentic architecture challenges like improving guardrails and security controls.

But cyber insurance company Navasana, which made the top five for the first time ever, was an example of a company indirectly focused on AI. Instead, Navasana launched to handle new risk dynamics that AI created, speaking to broader industry trends.

At one level, everyone's been thinking about cyber insurance for a long time, Ackerman adds. But looking at how policies are written in cyber, he has noticed a shift in risk as they add disclaimers and exemptions.

"What makes cyber attractive from an investment perspective is you never really solve it," Ackerman tells Dark Reading. "You never mitigate risk fully. It's a very hard puzzle piece to put together. The hope with AI is you get this real-time data to understand posture and environments. I still think there's a real lag though because insurance doesn't operate in real time."

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

Navasna marked the first cyber insurer to make the top five due to the end-to-end, continuous services it offers in a space where organizations manage such a broad umbrella of needs. As an early-stage investor, Ackerman is not looking to "feed the consensus machine" but wants to anticipate what's next. In venture capital, that's hard right now, he adds. Still, the conference and DataTribe Challenge look to showcase companies that are currently topical and addressing real needs.

Navasana is an example of more emerging needs, says Ackerman, while Sondera is in the "sweet spot" by addressing current challenges, as attacks make it clear that agentic AI needs more guardrails.

Sondera is "doing some really interesting things in that space that are well beyond what others are doing," says Scott. What resonated with the audience was how much research Sondera put into understanding what organizations actually need, he adds.

Rather than operating at the rule level, Sondera's approach starts at a much higher level, beginning with the human's underlying intent and what they're trying to achieve. Then organizations can work with users to generate the specific rules.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

It's increasingly evident that agents can be very persistent and act independently, so control is essential. That may be one reason that Sondera took home the trophy — people really understand the problems they've seen in their environments, Ackerman adds.

Ackerman sees two timelines in cybersecurity right now. Discussions over the past 18 to 24 months centered around concerns that offense has more of an advantage as attackers use AI to become faster and more advanced. Defense will catch up, but he believes that what the industry knows about cybersecurity — how to protect systems, and layer defense and zero trust — still work.

"We just have to apply them efficiently all the time," he urges.

The other timeline is what happens after 24 months. What issues will emerge then? Those are the core concepts, like protecting Internet infrastructure, that DataTribe wants to showcase in these events.

And the long-term lens is what the investors are betting on right now.

"It's not about what is going to get picked up in the next three to four months," Ackerman says. The startups and investments "have more of a five- to 10-year time horizon," he says.

One of Ackerman's favorite pastimes once startups wrap up their Challenge pitches is to walk around the floor while everyone's waiting for the judges to cast their votes and announce the winner. He considers the disconnect: He has spent weeks with the companies, coaching and prepping, yet the audience full of people from across the industry only get to know them for 20 minutes.

That's what makes storytelling so important, not just the cybersecurity and technical points. Learning what the judges and audience think of these companies is important for DataTribe, as well as for the startups which is the true value of cyber competitions.

For Ackerman, it's always great to hear that people had been thinking about a problem one of the contestants was trying to solve, but no one had developed a solution.

"That's validating," Ackerman says. "We're sort of directionally correct, which maybe in this market is the best you can do on any given day."

#9841. [$] Locking down hibernation for the winter

When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off. Unfortunately, the kernel does not have any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with, which is why lockdown, an optional kernel feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation. Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared a patch set that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.

#9839. Unattended reboots with encrypted disks

November 7, 2026 · About 7 minutes · Tags: blogsystem5, zkeys

This article was originally published on Substack in the Blog System/5 newsletter and is replicated here for archival purposes.

Do you run a small home server or NAS holding your precious photos and sensitive documents? If so, I suppose the drives are encrypted, right? But then… can you reboot the machine without manually entering a passphrase before being able to access your files again?

If you answered yes to the questions above—which is common for convenience—that implies the encryption keys live in the machine which… kinda defeats the purpose of disk encryption, doesn’t it? A thief can break into your house, lift the whole box (they are small these days, huh), plug it in elsewhere, and gain free rein over your files.

So, which one is it? Simplicity and reliability by allowing automatic reboots or data protection by keeping the key in your head? With ZKeys—a little new project I’m launching today—you can have your cake and eat it too.

A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC.

ZKeys is a managed service that stores encryption passphrases off-site. Client machines fetch the encryption keys from the service and keep those keys alive (unlocked) via periodic keepalive messages.

If the server stops receiving those messages for a long period of time (e.g. because it has been unplugged as part of theft), access to the key is automatically locked. You get automatic, passwordless reboots while keeping your data protected against real incidents.

About a year ago, I was reinstalling my FreeBSD home server to act as my NAS after a short stint with a Synology box. During that process, I decided to enable encryption for the ZFS data pool. But as I did that, I faced the question: how do I allow the machine to automatically serve my data after a reboot? I could put the key in a local file, which FreeBSD supports via the keylocation ZFS option, but that would render disk encryption pretty much useless.

So I had an idea: what if I put the key on a different machine away from my house? I could then make the NAS fetch the key to mount the drives. And if someone stole the server, I could wipe the remote key and make the data unreadable before they could plug it back in. I did post this to Twitter and there was some interest in the idea:

Silly or smart? I wrote a startup rc.d script to automatically mount my encrypted ZFS pool by fetching the key from a remote server. What I want to protect against is the "drives stolen from home" case. If that happened, I could quickly remove the key. https://t.co/eZle2nJlXW

But… did you notice the problem with what I said above? Wiping the key by hand after noticing something is wrong is problematic because the gap between those two events may be large. What if I’m on a long vacation and I have no means of noticing that the machine has been stolen? Game over.

So I refined the idea: what if I had a service that stored the key remotely and required the consuming machine to send it frequent pings to keep the key unlocked? This way, if the machine were stolen, it’d likely be offline for more than a few minutes and the service could automatically determine that something is wrong and lock the key from future accesses. And that’s precisely what ZKeys does.

Before getting into details, it’s important to get something out of the way early on: ZKeys is designed so that a compromise of the server is insufficient to retrieve or reconstruct your keys. This is done in two ways:

Split keys: The ZKeys server only stores half of the passphrase used to unlock a volume. The other half remains on the client machine. The zkeys client program combines both halves to produce the whole passphrase.

Encryption at rest: The keys are encrypted at rest with a password that the zkeys client must supply for retrieval and which is securely transmitted over HTTPS. The password only lives in the server’s memory for a brief period of time.

The tradeoff is, simply, that you MUST back up the full encryption keys in a third location of your own (a paper in a safe, a password manager, you name it). If ZKeys goes down or you lose your remote key password, there is absolutely nothing I can do to help you. You have been warned. The setup instructions later on will instruct you how to back the key up.

The ZKeys service is available at https://zkeys.jmmv.dev/ and the open-source client—along with system integrations for FreeBSD and Fedora—is in my jmmv/zkeys repository.

Disclaimer: ZKeys is offered to you for free. I make no promises about its reliability, availability, or anything else. I am giving you access because I expect that supporting a handful of extra users won’t be a big issue. But if support becomes a burden, or if load becomes unmanageable, I’ll have to re-evaluate my choices here. Which means that, for now, you have to use the limited LAUNCH50 code to get started!

The basic idea to set ZKeys up is the following:

That’s all it takes, but the steps are quite manual at the moment because no upstream OSes provide packages. The service documentation covers several scenarios in detail for FreeBSD and Fedora, so I’m not going to repeat them here.

Now for the nerdy details, because that’s what you’re here for:

The CLI is Rust, of course, but it has to come with a bunch of shell scripts to integrate with FreeBSD’s rc.d system and Fedora’s systemd and dracut. These integration points are the trickiest part of the client package and the hardest to validate automatically, which is why I only provide support for the two systems I use on a daily basis. It should be possible to integrate ZKeys with any other Unix-like OS, though.

The CLI package is a frankenmonster made up of Cargo and GNU Automake/Autoconf because of the above. I believe system-level tools should abide by de facto standard tooling even if such standard tooling is deficient, so GNU Autotools it is.

I run two non-replicated instances of the service: one in US West and one in EU West, because I have machines in both locations and both rely on encryption. I strongly suggest you use the US instance as I’m seeing frequent power hiccups in my EU deployment.

The frontend uses Bootstrap, straight from the 2010s. Does it look ugly? Maybe, but I kinda like it and, most importantly, it’s functional. Of course I could have asked AI to produce yet-another-dull-site full of gradients and slop, but I did not want to do that, so I stuck to what I already knew how to do by hand from previous services.

The admin page is an SPA, yes. This is an intentional design choice that forces a very clear separation between the backend APIs and the frontend. Whatever the current web frontend can do any other client can do as well. For example: the current zkeys CLI tool does not offer administrative operations but it could trivially be made to support them, because the APIs are right there.

The backend is built on my own III-IV framework which I’ve been building up over the last few years while implementing a couple of other services. I’ve had to add a lot more features to it to make this possible though.

Oops, I know that’s the name of a different effort, but you really need to encrypt your local drives. With computers becoming smaller and lighter every day, it’s easier than ever to steal them, and unfortunately home break-ins are common in some parts of the world. Block-level encryption is cheap in CPU terms, so do it. ZKeys just makes this process less cumbersome for headless servers.

Once again, head to https://zkeys.jmmv.dev/ to get started and use code LAUNCH50 to create an account!

And if you are interested in helping out, I’d appreciate the creation of packages for FreeBSD and Fedora, and integration scripts for other systems.

#9838. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for its AI Assistant

Nov 06, 2026 2 min read

Yelp has adopted a hybrid user interface architecture for its AI Assistant, combining native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering to support faster interface changes across platforms. The design uses Yelp’s CHAOS framework, short for Content Hosting Architecture with Optimization Strategies, to render conversation content while keeping navigation and message input native.

Yelp Assistant launched on iOS in 2024 to help users create project requests for local service professionals. It has since expanded to answer questions about businesses and support actions such as reservations, appointments, and food orders.

CHAOS supports web, iOS, and Android. In a server-driven UI architecture, the backend defines what the client displays and how it responds to interactions, so interface changes can reach users without requiring a new mobile app release.

Daniel Andrade Groppe, services tech lead at Yelp, highlighted,

Our existing CHAOS framework lacked some of the capabilities the Assistant required, including text input fields and network requests. Extending the framework would have delayed delivery, so we took a hybrid approach: we kept navigation and message input native while using CHAOS to render the conversation area.

Yelp Assistant UI: Native and Server-Driven Components (Source: Yelp Blog Post)

The implementation separates view configuration from conversation data. When a chat starts, the client fetches the CHAOS configuration and initializes a dataset for message events. Subsequent events update the existing view without refetching the configuration. Events represent persistent user and bot messages, temporary typing indicators and quick replies, and links that open destinations. The backend can also send actions to control the interface. For example, when a project request is complete, it can return a message, a link to view matches, and an action that disables chat input. This event-driven design decouples rendering from conversation logic.

Airbnb has documented a related approach through its Ghost Platform, which uses server-defined UI across web and mobile clients. Both approaches let teams update supported presentation without requiring every change to ship in a new client release. Yelp’s implementation applies this model to a conversational interface while retaining native controls and client-side handling for message state and interactions.

Yelp Assistant UI Chat Interaction Flow (Source: Yelp Blog Post)

The client displays submitted messages and a typing indicator, disables input, and sends requests to the backend. On response, it displays the reply and quick replies and re-enables input. Recoverable errors trigger retries, while non-recoverable failures disable input and prompt users to try again later.

Yelp engineers note that the architecture also introduces coordination challenges and engineers needed time to learn both the Assistant and CHAOS, and shared implementations can still behave differently across platforms. Separating view configuration from conversation data enables independent feature development. The architecture also supported reusing the Android Assistant to launch the Biz Ask Anything pilot. According to Yelp, this work laid the groundwork for its next-generation Assistant, which now connects business information with actions users can take.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

#9836. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.
