#9834. A bit about email

First, some terminology; A typical email will past through many different components on the way to the recipient:

(These aren't all necessarily different machines or even different programs, but it is helpful to name each step.)

The mail user agent (MUA) runs on the user's computer and is what they use to send or read messages. Let's say they send something: that message will be uploaded to to the submission agent (MSA) which checks the user's password before handing off to the mail transfer agent (MTA).

The transfer agent's job is to talk to other mail servers and get the message to the receiving side's MTA. Once received, it's given to the local delivery agent (LDA) to be stored until the recipient checks their email. The name "LDA" is non-standard, but I use it to avoid having four different abbreviations differing by a single letter.

The reason for this structure is that when the system was being designed (around 1980), most organizations could only afford a single server. Maintenance was a full time job and updates often required multiple days of downtime. A well-connected computer might have dedicated single-digits megabit/second link that worked half the time.

This forced the MTA and MUA distinction: if the recipient's server isn't up when the email is set, the sending MTA will save the message and re-attempt delivery later. This way, short outages don't cause bounced mail. Since the mail client is an interactive program the user runs, a separate message store is needed to keep the email until it can be read.

Most MTAs are configured to continue retrying a message for five days, usually with exponential backoff: mine will wait 5 minutes after the first failure, and increase the interval to one hour in prolonged outages.

The MSA and LDA have always existed in some capacity, but have gotten a lot more complicated when people started accessing email from their own computers instead or remotely logging onto a server.

Most communication happens over the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, including MTA-MTA delivery. To narrow it down a bit, I'll pretend do be an MTA sending email to blog@maurycyz.com.

The first step is to look up the receiving MTA for that domain:

Email is old enough to have it's own dedicated DNS record instead of using subdomain hacks or TXT abuse. The number is a priority (smaller is higher), which is used if multiple hosts are specified: a big email provider will have multiple servers to ensure timely delivery.

SMTP is a relatively straightforward text based protocol. The one catch is that most mail servers will require a CRLF as a data terminator. This can often be sent with ctrl-m, but using a tool that automatically inserts cartridge-return bytes is easier:

Each line sent is a command, to which the remote server responds with a three digit number followed by a human readable explaintaion. 200 responses mean it worked, 300 is "carry on...", 400 indicates temporary errors which tell the sender to try again later, 500 errors indicate that the email should be returned as un-deliverable.

(If this seems similar to HTTP, that's no coincidence. A lot of the web, including its header syntax, was lifted from SMTP)

The first command is always HELO (or EHLO), followed the sending MTA's hostname. This is usually not the same hostname that's in an email address, but many providers require it to match the sender's IP address. . The next two, MAIL FROM and RCPT TO specify the address to deliver to, and the address for any failure notifications. Bounce messages are usually generated one step up from where the error occurred: in most cases the receiving MTA has a problem and sends an error code to the sending MTA, but by that time MSA has already disconnect, forcing an emailed notification. Those notification themselves use an empty MAIL FROM to avoid infinite loops.

Once the address has been specified and accepted, a DATA command is sent, followed by the actual message. This, at a minimum, contains the "From" and "To" headers along with some text. The message is terminated with a lone period to which the server replies to indicate that the message was sucessfuly handed off.

Final hop MTAs should forward the email to the LDA before sending back a status code. This ensures that they never accept a message which they can't deliver, which would result in a error notification. This "backscatter" message interacts badly with spammers that forge MAIL FROM: it turns their obviously bogus message into one that is likely to be delivered and cause a nusance.

There is no requirement for the addresses inside the email to match the ones in MAIL FROM and RCPT TO (also known as the envelope). The most common cause of this is a mail that has been forwarded. For example, a mailing list will set the envelope destination to match each member's email, but keep the original "From" and "To" headers intact so that replies work correctly. The envelope from will usually be changed to point to somewhere the list administrator will check for error notifications.

Now, it's not that intermediate systems don't modify the headers: Most stages will add a "received" header to record where they got the message.

While required for MTA to MTA communication, SMTP is used throughout the whole system. The mail client submits email using a different port, but over the same protocol. Communication between internal components (i.e. MTA to LDA) often uses the closely related Local Mail Transfer Protocol: the main difference is the assumption that the receiver doesn't have a message queue and will either deliver the mail immediately or return an error.

Submission usually uses TLS to port 465, with the addition of a password (in base64):

AUTH PLAIN 334 AGh1bnRlcgBodW50ZXIy 235 2.7.0 Authentication successful

The one thing that's significantly different is the MUA's fetch, which operates on a "pull" basis. I won't go into the syntax here, but it's not terribly complicated.

... but if you actually try sending an email to, say, gmail, based on what I've written so far, it won't work. Some of that is due to them enforcing things like the Message-Id header: a unique identifier used to de-duplicate mail in cases where the receiving MTA accepts an email but the connection drops before the sender is informed about this. This causes the sender to try again later, which duplicating the message.

Base SMTP trusts that every sender is be well behaved: anyone can send email as anyone else. In fact, many hosts were configured to accept and relay mail from anyone as a conveyance for when someone's usual server was down.

The original solution to bad behavior was to get the culprit kicked off the internet... but that fell apart quickly once the network grew and companies began getting involved: the first documented case of spam email was sent in 1978 and sold 13 million dollars in computers. While authentication doesn't prevent spam, it makes it possible to filter out unwanted senders.

Verifying sender addresses is not possible using the MX record, since there is no guarantee the same host is used for receiving and sending mail. The simplest solution is to publish the sending address in a seperate DNS record:

@ TXT v=spf1 ip4:65.109.172.162 ip6:2a01:4f9:c011:841a:b01d::1 -all ; Roughly: ; allow from 65.109.172.162 ; allow from 2a01:4f9:c011:841a:b01d::1 ; deny otherwise

However, that's not quite enough for the email empire. Big-tech also wants the email body to be signed with a cryptographic key published via a (DKIM) DNS record. This requires adding a step to sending mails, usually as a plugin for the MTA.

While I rag on big-tech a lot, but this is actually a sensible policy: SPF can only verify the MAIL FROM, since forwarding the email will chance the source IP address. DKIM signatures are attached to the message and can be used to verify the original sender (the "From" address) of a message, which is what's actually shown to the user in most cases.

However, both of these don't actually prevent spam, because spammers can just set up a few TXT records. Big-tech also requires the sender's HELO hostname to be consistent with their IP address, via both forward and reverse DNS. This helps prevent compromised devices from spewing out junk: a smart TV is unlikely to have a meaningful PTR record, and if it does, that hostname won't resolve back to it's address.

... unfortunately this policy also makes it impossible to directly send mail from most residential internet connections unless you own the address block. Of course, the solution is to pay a big-tech company money to relay your emails. If you don't like this, find a mail provider with more permissive rules: the only reason big-tech is able to keep their racket running that five or so companies control 99% of email.

This is where SMTP stops being so simple. Let's look at the simplest possible email once it's been delivered:

Return-Path: Delivered-To: bob@here Received: from here by here with LMTP id bs05E10S7Go4VQMAHrglgg (envelope-from ) for ; Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:21:33 +0000 DKIM-Filter: OpenDKIM Filter v2.11.0 here B05E67CD18 Received-SPF: None (mailfrom) identity=mailfrom; client-ip=313.33.33.337; helo=there; envelope-from=alex@there; receiver=here Received: from there (unknown [313.33.333.337]) by here (Postfix) with SMTP id B05E67CD18 for ; Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:20:42 +0000 (UTC) From: alex@there To: bob@here Hello, World!

The format of the headers is superficially similar to HTTP headers, except that no line should exceed 78 bytes. (without the CRLF line terminator) Overlong headers are broken up and newly created lines are prefixed with whitespace to indicate that they are a continuation of the last header.

Mail software generally preppends headers to the start of a message, so it's helpful to read them backwards. "From" and "to" are fairly self explanatory. Next, the "received" header contains a note from the receiving MTA: it includes the source's HELO name, IP address, RCPT TO and a timestamp.

The MTA then performed SPF and DKIM checks, which came up empty: There's no signature and the MAIL FROM hostname is not publically resolvable.

The LDA added another "received" header, although it's not very helpful. More importantly, it tacked on the "return-path" with the original MAIL FROM address and recorded the mailbox the message was delivered to.

However, the body isn't always plain text. This is an email that includes formatting:

[...] MIME-Version: 1.0 Content-Type: multipart/alternative; boundary=----IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit ------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable Hello, World! I can do bold text! ------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

Hello, world! I can do bold<= /b> text
------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X--

However, since not all email clients can understand HTML, the message also includes a plain text version. This is done using MIME's "multipart" encoding, in this case, multipart/alternative, which indicates all the versions are functionally equivalent.

MIME's version number has been stuck at 1.0 since 1996.

The delimiter is a randomly chosen string, which allows multiple multiparts to be nested inside without escaping. Each section of the message has it's own headers, in this case, indicating that it's sent in the quoted-printable encoding. This allows the email message to contain any bytes without exposing the MTA to scary things like non-seven-bit ASCII: remember, the SMTP is 45 years old.

In quoted-printable, equal signs are used as the escape character: if followed by two hex digits, it decodes to that byte. If followed by a newline, both characters are removed. This is used to break long lines that could otherwise cause trouble.

In this email, "=3D" becomes a literal equal sign and both lines are joined together. If you've ever seen an email with stray equals or missing one or two characters ~ every 80 bytes, broken quoted-printable decoding is usually the culprit.

The second "content-transfer-encoding" is base64, which is used for binary files like attached images:

MIME-Version: 1.0 Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr" Content-Disposition: inline --5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii Content-Disposition: inline Check out this file: --5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr Content-Type: application/octet-stream Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="file.bin" Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64 J7mtSdbQItOAi345nwaNkkTXrnDIRPA0DSwhbSAOwm2C/KoHjQIotY9lnJRMBRk9InQaHOxL bb7DGd9EN6uRpjvCbox9xblAh3CxH7sl+YAkYcKw1V100RpBwMhgaXfUJBB3oRkLffgRwEyK v9qFBLp9zZ+SiRJoRWbA4aZLexPhHZ35vFROVKYtiAeMlD1s15v3kPZvEADam0e45BoSaqmp 1S3z3b5wBIFHJUxQULD589MKaFx2Z2A+91pl/pbZWmZkzt55D/hZ05kjUUbXUnDnTYAQE2Gk WnN+SnrQvfEO+Tz7AdrbLD1q2DgwWW+k0cVJLKjdwRxesGhAkQCZfHVrno6R4iXjTbInIbQv hXzQiV840iUiUhk282WADd1ffJ0sot2Waf7XHLIE1lZVFQ3iGofYbw8pZlg3sb35AnIWPZKv fbC6Yh95RV23R4K2NHeBX1rpl4bSSiftnD2RbsBzv7cgw/6M/Lj3O40NFGAaUC+J7TpAaXdi tvlPsNQhMo8QRf/ub7WK42cPUlz1fKq1k1pzGN96YOsE5azMfF4vLANtbtbVmLIp2WmgBk0P 9IGMWy/xIAe0cOh+bqzru2+ojJGgx9uX4VSTP9BaTOwkVX5+rQfpp1qJodtHiO8sHw6Pg+Mg WcpqQPC7118ccuT44cVpIRkwOSoJzsW++WM= --5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr--

This is why size limits are often disappointing: the email will be 33% larger than the attached file. More efficient encodings (raw binary data) are supported by some MTAs, but may have to be converted to base64 somewhere down the path... which would break DKIM signing.

No encoding ("7-bit") can be used if the message has short lines and fits in low-bit ASCII. However, "7-bit" is mostly seen as a null encoding for already encoded multipart containers. Quoted-printable if the message is mostly text, but has something that risks breaking ancient software. Base64 for binary data.

The SSL/TLS used by mail clients is effectively the same as for a browser: the mail provider must go to a certificate authority, prove their identity and get a certificate.. Algorithms and ciphers are disabled at the slightest hint they may be insecure.

However, MTAs operates on "trusted" networks... although it's less that an attacker can't get access to internet traffic, but that if they could, it would be possible for them to pass an ACME challenge and take out a trusted certificate.

As a result, the goal is mostly to protect against passive eavesdropping: most sysadmins don't bother dealing with a CA and use self-signed certificates. (it's not like CAs have a good track record: 4)

Another weird thing about email is that MTAs don't use a separate TLS port. All connections on port 25 start as plaintext, then the sender issues a STARTTLS command and hands over the connection to a SSL/TLS library. It's somewhat janky, but it allows servers to attempt to use encryption and cleanly fall back if it's not supported.

Such an approach isn't great for submissions, since a fall back would leak the password... and baddies on shared networks or nosy residential ISPs can strip out the STARTTLS command. For this case, it's best to default use the dedicated SSL submission port: 465.

(This port actually has a bit of a history, with it being deprecated in favor of STARTTLS before being re-endorsed once we realized using optional SSL for passwords was a bad idea.)

Unless you write email related software or run infrastructure, most of this information is profoundly useless. However, there are a few things you might want to remember.

The underlying protocols allow five days for delivery, and it can sometimes take longer. Since users expect delivery in seconds and most emails are at least somewhat time sensitive, some MTAs are configured to send out delay notification if a message is taking a while.

You may want to find out if yours does this before assuming the recipient is ignoring you.

A message will be stored and forwarded by multiple systems in plaintext. Anyone on the network path may be able to read your email: SSL/TLS is not universally supported and can trivially be stripped out by active attackers.

The lack of deniablity and forward secrecy can be excused as limitiations of email's store-and-forward architecture... but default plaintext and making no attempt to encrypt certain the subject line or attachments is a recipe for disaster: at least with vanilla email, people know it is not encrypted.

"Encrypted" email providers are largely snake oil. While the message store can encrypt messages and a custom MUA could decrypt them, the MTA must have access to plaintext. As a result, it provides minimal to no security against most attack vectors despite the "millitary grade encryption". The only way to fix email would be to get everyone to agree to switch to an end-to-end encrypted protocol... but the whole point of email is universal compatability: encrypted messaging can exist, but encrypted email is contradictory.

The best hope is to find a mail provider that can be trusted not to snoop messages. That is to say, not an Advertising company (google) or one that's been pushing hard for LLMs (microsoft / apple): both of these businesses create strong incentives to read your messages. Although you'll still have to hope whoever you are communicating with isn't beign snooped on by their provider.

Worse, DKIM signatures act as a lifelong proof that an email came from your provider's servers, even if a message is years old and has no clear chain of custody. This makes leaked, hacked, or snooped emails ideal extortion material: since the bad actor can trivially prove they haven't been fabricated.

This property, called non-repudiation, is generally not desirable for private messaging systems. Avoiding signing not an option if you want to interoperate with big-tech, but it is possible to regularly rotate and publish private keys. Before they key is published, the signature can be trusted to verify it is legitimate. However, once the key has been published, the signature can been forged by anyone and is rendered retroactively untrustworthy.

Since authentication is checked during delivery by the MTA and LDA, this doesn't affect how the email will be handled. However, it will cast doubt on the authenticity of leaked messages since the signature could have been forged with minimal effort.

While key rotation is common practice, most mail providers don't publish their old private keys, so the signature is still trustworthy (modulo the service being hacked). I would advise against emailing something you wouldn't be comfortable reading out in public.

#9833. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks, but it doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

#9832. One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The record theft shows how weak system separation, inadequate controls, and untested attack possibilities can turn one breach into systemic loss.

Last week's $6.3 billion breach at Binance underscores why effective security often depends not just on what an organization's controls are designed to block, but also on what they are configured to allow.

Details from Binance's disclosures thus far show that a threat actor, whom the FBI has identified as North Korea's TraderTraitor group, compromised a developer's laptop to access an internal service container with the permissions to initiate withdrawal requests.

Using that access as a starting point, the attackers exploited additional points of compromise and an Ethereum account-delegation mechanism to gain transaction approval authority over a hot wallet. And in around 20 minutes, the threat actors drained billions of dollars in assets.

In the process, the attackers appear to have bypassed Binance's normal approval controls. The company itself has said there's no evidence the attackers used any leaked wallet keys to carry out the massive theft.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

"Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an employee as the starting point. Its subsequent investigation has identified additional points of breach, showing the incident went beyond one device," the cryptocurrency exchange noted.

The incident, at least based on available details so far, has raised questions about whether Binance had sufficient independent safeguards to prevent a compromised system from approving and executing unauthorized withdrawals.

"At a minimum, a platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security so no single compromise, such as a hacked employee laptop, can authorize a transfer," says Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and director of security at NCC Group. "Those layers need to be independent of one another."

Funds, for instance, should be separated across hot and cold wallets to limit the impact of a compromise. Developers and administrators should have privileged access workstations to ensure systems they used for critical operations are separate from those they use for other activities such as email and Web browsing, he says. Also critical is 24/7 monitoring for anomalous behavior to help detect compromised endpoints and suspicious activity before attackers can exploit privileged access.

The focus should be on identifying single points of compromise, such as components or privileged roles whose compromise could give an attacker control over funds. "Protecting private keys is only part of the challenge. The systems that request and approve their use must also be secured. A properly secured system has layered, independent controls, hot/cold separation, and has been through threat modelling and end-to-end security testing," Rawlins says.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

For now, much remains unclear about exactly how the unauthorized transactions occurred and what safeguards Binance had in place to protect against them. Following the attack, the cryptocurrency exchange moved quickly to freeze some $3 billion. It has also claimed to have replenished — though not recovered — approximately 95% of the affected assets, meaning it has used its own funds to replace the stolen assets.

Cryptocurrency exchanges face many of the same threats as traditional financial institutions. But unlike banks and other financial institutions, which have long been subject to regulations governing operational risk and security, crypto exchanges have not yet faced the same level of oversight, making them a popular target for attackers.

John Bruggeman, vCISO at IT services firm CBTS, says large cryptocurrenct exchanges like Binance have to know that they are constantly being targeted by threat actors. In addition to controls that protect the perimeter or authenticate users, these companies also need to know what trusted identities and systems can do, verify high-impact actions, and prevent one compromised component from becoming a path to valuable assets.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

That means segregation of duties, management of private keys that authorize transfers, limits on the size of a transfer, MFA on the use of the private key monitoring, alerting for large transfers, and endpoint detection on all employee devices, Bruggeman says.

Also key is user behavior analysis for all users. Architecturally, organizations like Binance should have custody mechanisms for protecting the cryptocurrency and wallets themselves, transaction controls on how to move the cryptocurrency, some kind of rate limits on withdrawals, identity and access controls, and segregation of duties so no one user can initiate and also finalize a transfer, Bruggeman says.

The Binance breach is an important reminder of why all organizations need to test the path that attackers can potentially take after gaining initial access to an environment and not assume that individual controls, each working as they should, are sufficient protection, analysts said. "The entry point and the damage can sit very far apart, so stop grading your security by how well the front door holds," says Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at Secure.com.

The traditional approach to security is to check whether a request is valid. It almost never checks whether the action behind it should happen, he says. Available information suggests the attackers used Binance's own signing system to sign the transfers, so they looked valid on the way out. It was the "correct math, wrong decision," Ahmed says.

Security has to move from proving identity to governing consequences, he says. That means putting a human approval gate in front of any action that moves money or data, with limits that count across every system at once. "And test the whole route from laptop to payout, not each box on its own," Ahmed advises.

The Binance attack scenario can play out in any enterprise, too. "Swap out the withdrawal service for a payment system, a customer database, or a deployment pipeline, and this is an ordinary enterprise breach," he says. "A clean report from every tool you own tells you nothing about whether someone can walk from a laptop to the money, because no single tool is asked that question."

Robert Coles, senior manager of threat intelligence security at Black Duck, says the broader takeaway for organizations isn't really about cryptocurrency or the attack on Binance itself. Rather, it's about the blast radius, or what happens after initial break-in. It's one thing, he says, for an attacker to gain initial access. But turning that into a theft of billions of dollars is another entirely.

"Every organization has critical systems and privileged accounts where a compromise can have a much bigger impact," Coles says. "We spend a lot of time asking how we keep attackers out. We should spend just as much time asking, ‘If they do get in, what stops them next?'"

Security teams must assume something eventually will get compromised and make sure that one compromise doesn't become a catastrophic business event, Coles noted.

The Binance breach, the biggest ever by magnitude, is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange. In February 2025, Bybit lost approximately $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency after attackers manipulated a transaction approval process involving an Ethereum cold wallet. In May 2019, Binance itself lost 7,000 bitcoin after attackers obtained user API keys and two-factor authentication codes to bypass existing security checks. In October this year, attackers compromised a third-party script on Polymarket's website and used it to move funds from some user wallets.

North Korean threat actors have been especially aggressive in targeting crypto exchanges and wallets in general and account for 76% of all the money that traders have reported as stolen so far in 2026. In six of the past nine years, groups from the cash-strapped nation have accounted for at least one-third of all reported cryptocurrency theft.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. #9831. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

InfoQ Homepage News Varlock Releases Bumpy: a File-Based Versioning Alternative to Changesets

Nov 07, 2026 2 min read

Bumpy, a modern monorepo-friendly version management and changelog tool from the team behind Varlock, has been gaining traction as a self-described successor to changesets. First unveiled in April 2026 via a Show HN post from creator Theo Ephraim, the project now ships under the @varlock/bumpy package and claims to address more than 120 open issues from its predecessor.

Bumpy follows the familiar changesets workflow. Contributors drop a small markdown "bump file" into .bumpy/ that declares which packages should be released, at what level, with a changelog description. The files are reviewable in the PR diff, consolidated into a release PR by CI, and consumed when that PR merges. An example looks like this:

Where the two tools diverge is beneath that surface. Bumpy ships with full support for workspace: and catalog: protocols across npm, pnpm, Yarn and Bun, per-package custom publish commands for VS Code extensions, Docker images or JSR targets, and a configurable three-phase dependency propagation algorithm that lets teams decide how peer dep bumps cascade through their graph. The CI story is leaner too, with two commands, bumpy ci check and bumpy ci release, running directly in a standard GitHub Actions workflow with no GitHub App to install or separate action repo to trust.

Version 1.14 added branch-based prerelease channels where prerelease versions are derived at publish time and never committed to git. The design targets complaints documented in the changesets own prerelease docs, which describe their pre mode as "very complicated" with states that are "very hard to fix". Another differentiator is AI integration. Bumpy ships an agent skill that teaches LLMs how to inspect git changes, identify affected packages and generate bump files via bumpy add. It installs through the Vercel Labs skills CLI, the GitHub CLI, or as a Claude Code plugin.

Getting started is a single install and an init that migrates existing changesets projects automatically:

A Show HN thread was candid that the project "was coded using AI, but carefully", and the team notes it is already being used to release Varlock alongside 25+ related libraries and plugins. In a separate thread on polyglot monorepos, bumpy was mentioned as a tool that "fixes a few things with changesets around custom publishing". Teams evaluating migration have opened issues flagging gaps such as Yarn 4.10 catalog detection.

Competition tightened with the changesets v3 release in August 2026, which closed many of the long-standing issues bumpy originally targeted. Bumpy's own differences doc now compares against v3 and credits it as "a substantial cleanup", while pointing out remaining gaps around configurable propagation, catalogs, custom publish targets and prerelease workflows. Relative to semantic-release, bumpy keeps the file-based model but adds a bumpy generate command that can produce bump files from branch commits when teams want to bridge both styles.

Bumpy is MIT-licensed, built in TypeScript, and available via the @varlock/bumpy package on npm, with the full source and documentation on GitHub.

#9828. 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

Evidence suggests a model may have generated and revised commands during the ransom gang's breach, though researchers stopped short of claiming full automation.

A 3AM ransomware attack targeting a UK school estate may provide an early look at how cybercriminals could use AI as a force multiplier rather than a replacement for human operators.

Bitdefender today published research concerning a "hybrid AI ransomware attack" observed in the wild, attributing certain actions taken to human or agentic elements. On the surface, the attack is fairly straightforward. As a blog post explained, a 3AM ransomware affiliate attacked a school in the UK, "then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools."

Attackers stole backup credentials, created rogue domain-admin accounts, established trusts between previously separate Active Directory domains, moved between schools, stole data, and deployed 3AM ransomware. In other words, the attack largely followed a familiar ransomware playbook, despite Bitdefender's claims that AI helped execute parts of the operation.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

Where the attack got more interesting was how, as the security vendor argued, it didn't fit neatly into pre-existing buckets for attacks involving AI. It wasn't exactly an AI-generated attack where the malware was fully or largely created by a large language model (LLM); it wasn't exactly an AI-assisted attack where human engineers built the tools while using AI to speed up work; and it wasn't exactly an AI-operated attack where the LLM orchestrates actions and runs the show, as it were.

In this case, Bitdefender argued an AI system appeared to handle repetitive command generation and troubleshooting while a human operator made high-level decisions.

Many elements of the attack were ordinary for ransomware, such as significant use of living-off-the-land (LOTL) techniques, where attackers abuse tools already present on the victim's machine rather than relying on malware — in this case PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), reg, netsh, rundll32, and other domain and scheduling utilities preinstalled on Windows. The attacker also used "an Impacket-style remote-execution tool," as well as Mimikatz and a previously published Veeam script.

But despite the attack's ordinary nature, Bitdefender assessed that several things suggest the use of an agentic loop, the control structure that makes an AI agent work. Certain actions appeared to be taken by a program rather than a human operator.

"The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software's web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual (Veeam REST API authorization), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script," the blog post read. "The retries behave like a loop too."

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

In another example, researchers assessed that the time taken between PowerShell command attempts was shorter than a human would take if issuing them by hand, but longer than if an LLM was orchestrating by itself. The longer time taken between individual tasks but the shorter time between retries "is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries."

Bitdefender caveated its findings by noting that it was unable to access the machine the attacker worked from, so it couldn't document anything tangible involving the AI model itself. The research acts as an argument that this attack behaves like a human operating alongside an agent, which is a working model defenders may wish to plan around.

With that in mind, Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender, tells Dark Reading that "a hybrid model is more reasonable for financially motivated cybercriminals, technically and economically, than a fully autonomous attack."

Related:Foul Language: WordlistLoader Disguises Malware as Ordinary Text

But even as a one-off, the situation is notable because the primary victim was an organization in a critical sector, and Bitdefender's anecdote suggests the affiliate may have used an AI agent to scale the attack by handling repetitive troubleshooting and command generation, although the report stops short of showing AI-enabled capabilities the attacker otherwise lacked.

Moreover, other similar institutions could fall in the crosshairs. "From a domain controller it enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL (the shared folder where Active Directory stores logon scripts, readable by any domain user) for the names and subnets of other schools," according to the research blog post.

The good news is that because much of this attack followed the typical ransomware playbook, the defender recommendations that stop regular ransomware would also stop the attack described in this research.

Zugec adds that agentic loops are noisy from an indicator standpoint, as many of their actions are repetitive and brute force in nature. "An agentic loop doesn’t make an attack quiet; it makes it repetitive: the same command re-run, small tweaks, numbered scripts and probe files left on disk. Even the quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. 'Machine speed' is mostly a marketing phrase about very expensive incidents; in real attacks, especially with local models, we expect this slower and noisier pattern. Speed isn't the giveaway; repetition is."

The vendor recommends focusing on prevention: Keep admin credentials of different domains separate, treat backups as a possible target, restrict remote execution and administrative shares to known management hosts, block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them, and put endpoint security tooling on every machine.

"Prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed," the blog post read, "because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth."

In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. #9826. LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Cybercriminals have turned reselling cloud access to LLMs into a lucrative business model, with some victims paying as much as $1 million in resource consumption before access was revoked.

Cybercriminals have created a thriving business model out of stealing cloud access to commercial large language models (LLMs) and reselling it to paying customers, with the resource cost for victims reaching high as $1 million before access to their LLM was revoked.

The practice, called LLMjacking, has been around almost as long as LLMs themselves. However, now it's become an illicit enterprise on the underground market, providing a lucrative source of revenue for cybercriminals while victims are left to absorb the high cost of model usage, according to a report published Monday by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant.

LLMjacking can create a massive spike in computing resources in a matter of hours, differentiating it from its more well-known cousin, cryptojacking, which gradually consumes resources. This has made it an attractive revenue stream for "a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally," Google researchers shared in the report.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

"Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked," they wrote.

The report details how attackers gain initial access to LLMs and achieve persistence on targeted networks, and describes the service model around LLMjacking that has become a lucrative endeavor for cybercriminals.

To gain initial access to an organization's LLM, attackers typically identify publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtain valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys, according to Google.

"The dominant initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens — including identity and access management (IAM) credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens (PATs), and active session tokens — which threat actors leverage to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure," the researchers wrote.

Some attackers also deliberately keep their initial activity quiet to gain access to an organization's LLM, according to Google. The researchers observed the use of minimal API requests, sometimes containing just one output token, to validate stolen credentials without generating significant consumption.

This sneaky way to gain and then sell access to the LLM could mean organizations are giving up valuable resources without even knowing, while the attacker is cashing in, notes Nick Tausek, lead security automation architect at agentic AI firm Swimlane.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

"By the time someone asks why the cloud bill has exploded, the attacker may already have paying customers," he says. "Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important."

This notably represents a detection challenge for organizations that need to identify early indicators of compromised identities, unauthorized permissions, and suspicious access to AI services rather than just look for unusual consumption, he says.

The report outlines several examples of how attackers compromised and LLMjacked organizations, demonstrating that there is not just one route to take for successfully and illicitly gaining access to an LLM.

In the middle of the year, for example, a threat cluster tracked as UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used it to grant further access to an LLM API. Attackers also hosted a session hijacking page mimicking an application portal to join a group of LLM users.

"This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls," the researchers explained.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

In another instance, a threat actor gained initial entry by combining a stolen personal access token (PAT) to access private code repositories and a suspected Web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment.

Similarly, a different threat actor used compromised cloud federation tokens to programmatically generate new access keys that allowed the attacker to bypass MFA protections, according to Google.

Once access to an LLM has been gained, it then needs to be sold for attackers to make money. The key to this part of the LLMjacking business model is what is called an LLM Mixer, which is an underground service that turns stolen access to commercial AI models into a subscription business, according to Google. These services aggregate compromised credentials, route customer requests through victim environments, and offer access to premium models at prices significantly below legitimate market rates.

As the researchers describe it, LLM mixers act as illicit middlemen, allowing cybercriminals to resell access to compromised enterprise LLM accounts without their customers needing their own legitimate API credentials or cloud infrastructure.

"In one investigation, GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure, demonstrating the sophisticated specialization emerging in this space," the researchers wrote.

Indeed, LLM Mixers are an important part of the emerging LLMjacking ecosystem because they provide the monetization layer that makes stealing enterprise AI access financially attractive.

Since LLMjacking relies on victims being unaware for as long as possible, the key to not getting dinged with a huge resource-consumption bill is to catch on as quickly as possible to the intrusion.

To do this, defenders should prioritize IAM and supply chain security, two of the most common pathways for gaining access to and abusing cloud services, according to Google.

Other best practices for preventing LLMjacking in a cloud environment include good credential hygiene by using a centralized secrets-management platform; least privilege by ensuring users and service accounts only possess the permissions necessary for their specific role and required tasks; and code monitoring by automating secret scanning within codebases such as GitHub and GitLab.

Routine configuration audits, rate limiting, network allow listing, budget alerts, and MFA are also good defense strategies, according to Google.

#9825. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

InfoQ Homepage News Open Source pg_vectorsearch Brings More Scalable Vector Search to PostgreSQL

Nov 07, 2026 3 min read

Tiger Data has released pg_vectorsearch, an open source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search, currently in alpha. Its PRISM index uses data partitioning and compression instead of the graph-based approach used by pgvector’s HNSW index, reducing memory requirements and index build times.

According to the authors, pg_vectorsearch enables faster, more memory-efficient vector search directly in PostgreSQL, reducing the infrastructure required to handle large vector datasets. The extension supports existing pgvector columns, allowing applications to perform vector search without a separate database. To use the new capabilities, developers must install the extension and create a PRISM index on the vector column:

In Tiger Data’s own benchmarks using 100 million vectors, PRISM built an index in 1 hour and 40 minutes on a machine with 128 GB of memory, while HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) took 42 hours on a machine with 512 GB of memory. Formerly known as Timescale, Tiger Data is the company behind TimescaleDB, the open source PostgreSQL extension for time-series data and real-time analytics.

Erik Nordström, senior staff engineer at Tiger Data, Matvey Arye, principal engineer at Tiger Data, and Noah Hein, staff product marketing manager at Tiger Data, write:

PRISM brings a partition-based approach to PostgreSQL, similar to the approach used by newer dedicated vector search systems. Instead of connecting every vector to its neighbors in a graph, PRISM groups similar vectors into partitions and stores them as a list in a compressed format that is densely packed into database pages.

While HNSW is an approximate nearest-neighbor algorithm that quickly finds vectors similar to a query in large datasets, PRISM narrows searches to relevant partitions and scans compressed vectors sequentially. This reduces index size and avoids costly random memory or disk access, enabling faster vector search with less RAM directly in PostgreSQL.

Michael Freedman, cofounder and CTO of Tiger Data, published an article describing the architecture of the PRISM vector index. The index in pg_vectorsearch combines hierarchical clustering to narrow the search space, compressed vectors for efficient sequential scanning, and RaBitQ quantization to reduce expensive distance calculations. It duplicates vectors near partition boundaries to improve recall and relies on PostgreSQL’s native storage, logging, and concurrency mechanisms.

Incremental rebalancing is not yet fully implemented, so frequent data changes may require rebuilding the index to maintain search efficiency. Freedman explains:

The harder problem is maintaining the clustering as the dataset changes. Centroids don't automatically move when new vectors arrive, and posting lists gradually lose their original physical locality. We currently support limited on-demand splitting of oversized posting lists for flat indexes, but the more general rebalancing operations, including merging and reassignment, are not implemented yet.

In a popular Hacker News thread, the overall reaction is one of technical interest but caution. Practitioners see potential in faster vector search with lower memory requirements inside PostgreSQL, but raise questions about independent benchmark validation, whether pg_vectorsearch could replace pgvectorscale, and the lack of support for filtered searches. Hermon Hagos comments:

Vector search just got cheaper (...) For those of us building RAG apps on one database and a tight budget, that matters. Fast semantic search without spinning up a separate vector store or a bigger server is real money saved. It is still alpha, so do not ship it to clients yet, but this is one to watch closely.

Although not independently validated, Tiger Data’s benchmarks use an open source tool, measure recall@10 against exact search results, and compare both indexes under the same PostgreSQL configuration and instance types, using pgvector’s 16-bit halfvec for HNSW.

The new vector extension requires PostgreSQL 18 or later and currently supports vectors with up to 1968 dimensions. Filtered vector searches combining WHERE and ORDER BY are not supported until general availability. The project's code is available on GitHub. Tiger Data plans to move its existing pgvectorscale extension into maintenance mode.
