#9788. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9785. What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from an ill-conceived phishing simulation to a hacktivist attack on a US government agency.

Phishing tests can be an important part of cybersecurity awareness training. But as the NBA champion New York Knicks recently showed, they can also go awry.

According to a recent report in The Athletic, Madison Square Garden (MSG) Sports, which owns the Knicks, deployed a poorly timed and ill-conceived phishing simulation ahead of its banner-raising ceremony on Oct. 20. MSG Sports sent out emails to employees with offers of free championship rings commemorating the team's historic NBA Finals victory in June.

Team employees often receive championship rings at the start of the following season. However, the emails in this case were part of a phishing simulation, and when employees clicked on the links to select their rings, they were informed they failed the test and had to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. And they didn't get the rings, either.

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: a hacktivist group breached the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and published personnel records for more than 40,000 employees, and it's unclear how the agency was compromised; and a New York Times report claims a NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset.

#9783. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9782. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

Related:SecurityDataPipeline.com Launches as a New Educational Resource for the AI Era

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9779. Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

A operação, que contou com o uso de inteligência artificial, utilizou e-mails falsos, documentos governamentais falsificados e a criação de uma organização local para atacar escolas no Peru e no Equador, entre outras ações.

This translation was generated with our internal AI tool.

Uma operação de influência sediada na Rússia enviou e-mails se passando por autoridades educacionais do Peru e do Equador, levando algumas escolas a realizar eventos que os operadores então utilizaram para alimentar controvérsias, de acordo com um relatório divulgado pela OpenAI.

A operação de “fachada falsa”, apelidada de “Dark Clark,” utilizou uma combinação de planejamento baseado em IA e relatórios, além de técnicas mais tradicionais, para convencer administradores escolares a celebrar um “Dia Nacional da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística” em 21 de maio e a destacar três figuras políticas ucranianas, que foram então usadas para tentar semear divisão, afirmou a OpenAI em uma análise do uso operacional de seus modelos de IA. Em outras campanhas, como as direcionadas à Argentina e à Bolívia, as operações russas pareciam ter como objetivo influenciar a política local.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Os supostos operadores russos utilizaram IA para tornar seu fluxo de trabalho mais eficiente, redigindo relatórios internos sobre suas atividades e, em alguns casos, criando conteúdo para suas campanhas, informou a empresa.

“A IA pode conferir a essas operações de fachada maior escala, eficiência, fluência linguística e capacidade editorial”, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. “Os operadores podem usar essas vantagens para explorar vítimas desavisadas, como funcionários ou editores, e divulgar seu conteúdo para públicos que não têm ideia de quem está por trás disso, nem quais são suas motivações.”

A América Latina tornou-se um palco cibernético de espionagem e operações de influência na disputa entre as principais potências globais, tornando-se a região mais atacada ciberneticamente no mundo. Atores conhecidos ligados à China tiveram como alvo tanto a Venezuela quanto o Panamá no início deste ano para obter informações sobre a política na região e proteger os interesses petrolíferos do país. A Rússia expandiu suas operações de inteligência cibernética e desinformação, principalmente para frustrar os esforços dos EUA na região, de acordo com um relatório da RAND de 2026.

“A Rússia também mantém capacidades cibernéticas para realizar invasões direcionadas e desinformação com o objetivo de semear divisão política, perturbar a percepção da situação e enfraquecer as mensagens dos EUA em situações de crise”, afirmou o relatório da RAND.

A operação russa parece estar ligada a uma entidade conhecida como “Politology” ou “La Compania”, que tem vínculos com o falecido oligarca russo Yevgeniy Prigozhin, com o objetivo de influenciar a política global, de acordo com a análise da OpenAI. Os relatórios fornecidos ao modelo de IA continham informações detalhadas sobre as operações do grupo, incluindo detalhes sobre trabalhos anteriores que os ligavam aos grupos de Prigozhin.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

O ataque de desinformação contra escolas em Lima, no Peru, foi uma das campanhas descritas pelos atacantes. Ao elaborar uma diretiva com aparência oficial para os administradores escolares, citando um fictício “Dia da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística”, eles solicitaram que os alunos participassem de atividades de 10 a 15 minutos para aprender sobre três figuras políticas ucranianas. Posteriormente, os operadores instruíram os administradores a enviar fotos do evento.

A OpenAI investigou os eventos e encontrou detalhes que corroboravam as alegações dos operadores, disse Ben Nimmo, pesquisador-chefe da equipe de inteligência e investigações da OpenAI, à Dark Reading. O Ministério da Educação do Peru emitiu uma carta oficial (em espanhol) dois meses depois, mencionando a diretiva e informando que a embaixada da Ucrânia havia identificado a fraude em sua própria carta, datada de 25 de maio.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

“Nunca se deve acreditar em um agente de ameaças pelo que ele diz, certo?”, diz Nimmo. “ Para cada alegação, buscamos evidências na internet que a corroborassem. Para algumas das alegações que eles fizeram, simplesmente não conseguimos encontrar evidências. Talvez tenham sido removidas, talvez estivessem em lugares que não seriam encontrados por meio de uma busca em fontes abertas, talvez nunca tenham acontecido.”

Uma diretiva fraudulenta enviada às escolas de Lima, no Peru, por supostos agentes de desinformação russos. Fonte: Ministério da Educação do Peru (traduzido pelo Claude Opus 5.5)

Como a operação resultou em um político na Polônia citando os eventos, a OpenAI classificou o sucesso com nota 5 na Escala de Impacto de Operações de Influência de seis pontos.

Os operadores russos usaram técnicas semelhantes para induzir escolas no Equador a realizar uma cerimônia de juramento de lealdade ao presidente Daniel Noboa e a Erik Prince, ex-chefe da empresa militar privada Blackwater, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. Algumas escolas seguiram a orientação, o que levou a cobertura jornalística e uma denúncia oficial por parte do Ministro da Educação.

Os operadores alegaram ter conduzido com sucesso outras operações de influência das quais a OpenAI não conseguiu encontrar evidências, incluindo a divulgação de uma história de que uma influenciadora brasileira nas redes sociais teria sido traficada para a Ucrânia e a disseminação de um trecho de áudio que alegava que bancos bolivianos pretendiam limitar saques em dinheiro. Os operadores também, ocasionalmente, pediam ao ChatGPT para encontrar incidentes regionais pelos quais pudessem assumir o crédito, diz Nimmo.

Os operadores russos criaram uma chamada “plataforma de pesquisa”, denominada Social Research Center, que contratava funcionários regionais para criar conteúdo local, sem que eles soubessem que a organização fazia parte de uma iniciativa de desinformação.

Embora as operações tivessem como alvo a América Latina, a intenção era prejudicar as relações entre a Ucrânia e o resto do mundo, afirma Nimmo, da OpenAI.

“A maneira como eu encaro essa operação como um todo é que ela gira em torno da Ucrânia”, diz ele. “Trata-se de fazer a Ucrânia parecer mal.”

De modo geral, o uso da IA não abriu novos caminhos para ataques nem criou novas oportunidades de desinformação, mas a tecnologia fez com que as traduções para o idioma nativo soassem mais naturais, permitiu que os operadores assumissem papéis específicos com mais facilidade e simplificou o fluxo de trabalho da operação, afirma Nimmo.

“Se você pensar na Agência de Pesquisa na Internet e no inglês desleixado deles, acho que a IA realmente oferece uma vantagem incremental”, diz ele. “Mas não tenho a impressão de que o uso do nosso modelo tenha sido o fator decisivo. De certa forma, o manual de táticas era muito, muito tradicional.”

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9778. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#9777. UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Britain's new Labour-led government is making a concerted push to get ahead of the AI risks to its national networks and the industrial complex.

At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9776. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our demos, download our open models, and see how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#9775. Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Europe's supermarket freezer hacks show how security issues can cascade across an industry, disrupting supply chains at scale.

The recent refrigerator hacks wreaking havoc across European supermarkets is a lesson in how shared weaknesses in operational technology (OT) can spread across a whole supply chain.

On the night of Oct. 11, an unknown attacker reportedly compromised refrigeration controls used by hundreds of French supermarkets, triggering extended defrost cycles in refrigerators and freezers across the country. The incident caused millions of euros in damage across roughly 700 affected stores in France alone, spoiling food, damaging equipment, and even reportedly starting some fires in the process.

The technology leveraged in these attacks included Danfoss refrigeration controllers, as well as Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems. It's unclear how the threat actor gained access to these systems.

However, the Danfoss controllers at the center of this campaign ran Internet-accessible Web servers. Many were accessible using default login credentials: "admin" as the username and the current date as the password. CERT-FR made a number of recommendations in an advisory to affected supermarkets, such as changing default passwords, factory resetting compromised equipment, and updating firmware. Though to that last point, Danfoss told AFP that many of the attacks involved legacy products that no longer receive updates.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

What stands out about the French supermarket attacks is how a shared weakness in refrigeration infrastructure appears to have enabled disruption across hundreds of stores. While investigators have not publicly confirmed the initial access vector, the incident raises questions about the risks created when organizations rely on similar technologies, deployment models, and remote-access practices.

Chris St. Myers, director of SentinelLABS, says evidence suggests a common exposure problem, rather than market concentration, may have facilitated this issue.

"CERT-FR confirmed that the French compromises involved Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, along with Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. These technologies are deployed across many retail environments, often with similar remote access requirements and configurations," St. Meyers says. "That creates opportunities for attackers to reuse the same techniques across otherwise unrelated organizations."

Thomas Plank, CEO of industrial security firm Tributech, similarly diagnosed common exposure as a core issue behind the attacks.

"What's concentrated is the setup. Across chains and countries, it's the same model: remote-management controllers reachable from the internet, often on out-of-support firmware, maintained by a small number of contractors who look after hundreds of stores from one place," Plank tells Dark Reading. "When everyone runs the same risky pattern through the same few channels, one way in reaches many retailers at once, across borders, overnight. That's why this looks like a campaign rather than a string of unlucky stores."

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

It's highly unusual and hardly precedented for a cyberattack to have such a significant impact on the food supply chain, but it's not the only incident like it in recent memory.

A similar attack hit refrigeration and freezer systems in stores across other countries at the beginning of November, including Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. Around the same time, attackers targeted the refrigeration of three blood banks operated by the national French Blood Establishment, though the attack was stopped before blood plasma was damaged.

For as alarming and impactful these incidents may seem, supply chain targeting has become more common in recent years with 2021's Colonial Pipeline attack, Iran's recent targeting of fuel monitoring systems around the US, and 2024's Change Healthcare incident.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

The danger is clear, especially in the context of a supermarket. Piotr Buliński, chief technology officer (CTO) of Internet of Things (IoT) device management firm Qbee, says a supermarket chain runs thousands of small, unattended OT systems between refrigeration, HVAC, and building management. "Each one is 'just a few controllers,' so nobody treats them as critical infrastructure," he says. "Yet when they fail, the damage is immediate and physical."

These incidents remind us once again about the importance of securing critical infrastructure.

Updating OT systems is a challenging task in their own right because of the downtime often required. Much of the critical technology holding up industrial processes is intended to operate for years (if not decades) on end, while the organizations relying on OT can often include those too under-resourced to have dedicated security staff, like municipalities, or indeed, supermarkets.

Even as these problems have gotten a little easier to address over the years and many dedicated firms have risen to address these challenges, organizations still struggle to secure OT.

St. Meyers believes retail OT has historically received less security attention than traditional industrial environments, despite carrying many of the same underlying risks. He says this is possibly in part because refrigeration, HVAC, and building management systems are "often deployed and maintained outside the traditional IT security organization," despite being OT.

Plank agrees. He says one solution for retailers is to verify commands at the device level against engineering limits, as "no freezer should ever accept a command to go to 50°C, whoever sends it and whatever channel it arrives on," referencing the extreme temperatures some targeted equipment reached during the attacks.

For organizations outside the sphere of influence that want to learn from what happened here, there are several lessons: Don't use default passwords, take inventory of where and how industrial technologies are internet accessible, remove internet exposure wherever possible, and make sure all points of access are secured.

Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, tells Dark Reading that generally, this incident should be seen as a warning to retailers. "Industrial systems, from energy production to water management to food refrigeration, must be secured," he says, "and at a minimum not accessible to malicious hackers via the Internet."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

#9774. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 9, 2026

There's barely any of the Moon visible tonight as it approaches the New Moon. With less than a sliver illuminated, there is nothing for us to see in the way of lunar features.

As of Monday, Nov. 9, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the New Moon phase, with 0% of its surface visible.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

It takes the Moon around 29.5 days to pass through a complete lunar cycle. As it travels around Earth, the angle at which sunlight reaches its surface changes what we can see from here, producing the different phases, from the New Moon through to the Full Moon and back again. The cycle then starts over, as explained by NASA.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.
